stem_md:
Find all real numbers  $x$  which satisfy  $\frac{n}{3n+1}\leq x\leq \frac{4n+1}{2n-1}$ , for all  $n\in\mathbb{N}^*$ .

*Gheorghe Boroica*
solution_md: We need to find all real numbers  $x$  which satisfy  $\frac{n}{3n+1}\leq x\leq \frac{4n+1}{2n-1}$  for all  $n \in \mathbb{N^*}$ . Now,  $$ P=\frac{n}{3n+1}=\frac{1}{3+\frac{1}{n}} $$    $$ Q=\frac{4n+1}{2n-1}=2+\frac{3}{(2n-1)} $$  As  $n$  increases,  $P$  increases and  $Q$  decreases. Thus,   $$  \lim_{n \to \infty}P =\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{3+\frac{1}{n}} =\frac{1}{3}  $$     $$  \lim_{n \to \infty}Q= \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(2+\frac{3}{(2n-1)}\right)=2 $$  Thus,  $\boxed{x \in \bigg[\frac{1}{3},2\bigg]}$   $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
Let there be  $2n+1$  distinct points on a circle. Consider the set of distances between any two out of the  $2n+1$  points. What is the smallest size of this set?

*Radu Bumbăcea*
solution_md:
The answer is  $n$ .

Let the points be  $A_1$ ,  $A_2$ ,  $\dots$ ,  $A_{2n+1}$  in this order and let  $A_{n+1}^*$  be the antipode of  $A_{n+1}$ . By PhP, there are  $n$  points on the same side of  $A_{n+1}A_{n+1}^*$  so if we connect these points with  $A_{n+1}$  we will find  $n$  different lengths. For the construction take a regular  $2n+1$  gon.

solution_md:
Let $a,b,c$ be three positive real numbers with $ab+bc+ca=4$ . Find the minimum value of the expression $$ E(a,b,c)=\frac{a^2+b^2}{ab}+\frac{b^2+c^2}{bc}+\frac{c^2+a^2}{ca}-(a-b)^2. $$
By Bergstrom $$ \sum_{cyc}\frac{a^2+b^2}{ab}-(a-b)^2=6+\sum_{cyc}\frac{(a-b)^2}{ab}-(a-b)^2\geq6+\frac{(a-b+b-c+c-a)^2}{ab+ac+bc}-(a-b)^2=6. $$ The equality occurs for $a=b=c$ , which says that we got a minimal value.
$$ \sum_{cyc}\frac{a^2+b^2}{ab}-(a-b)^2=6+\sum_{cyc}\frac{(a-b)^2}{ab}-(a-b)^2\geq6+\frac{(a-b+c-b+a-c)^2}{ab+ac+bc}-(a-b)^2=6. $$

stem_md:
Consider the plane vectors  $\overrightarrow{OA_1},\overrightarrow{OA_2},\dots ,\overrightarrow{OA_n}$  with  $n\geq 3$ . Suppose that the inequality   $$ \big|\overrightarrow{OA_1}+\overrightarrow{OA_2}+\dots +\overrightarrow{OA_n}\big|\geq \big|\pm\overrightarrow{OA_1}\pm\overrightarrow{OA_2}\pm\dots \pm\overrightarrow{OA_n}\big| $$   takes place for all choiches of the  $\pm$  signs. Show that there exists a line  $\ell$  through  $O$  such that all points  $A_1,A_2,\dots ,A_n$  are all on one side of  $\ell$ .

*Cristi Săvescu*
solution_md: <details><summary>Sol.</summary>We choose  $O$  as the origin. Writing the position vectors we get   $$ |a_1+a_2+\dots+a_n|\geq|\pm a_1\pm a_2\pm\dots\pm a_n|. $$  Notice that   $$ |a_1+a_2+\dots+a_n|\geq|-a_1+a_2+\dots+a_n| $$    $$ |a_1+a_2+\dots+a_n|\geq|+a_1-a_2+\dots+a_n| $$    $$ \cdots $$    $$ |a_1+a_2+\dots+a_n|\geq|+a_1+a_2+\dots-a_n| $$  If we square all those relationships and then remove the similar terms we get that   $$ 2a_k\sum a_i\geq0,\, \forall\,k\in\overline{1, n} $$  Let  $G$  be the center of mass of the quadrilateral, then  $$ 0\leq a_k\frac{\sum a_i}{n}=|a_k|\big|\frac{\sum a_i}{n}\big|\cos{A_kOG}\Rightarrow \angle A_kOG\leq 90^\circ. $$  If we take  $\ell$  the line perpendicular to  $OG$  which passes through  $O$  then every point is on the same side of  $\ell$  as  $G$  (because of  $A_kOG\leq 90^\circ$ ), therefore we are done.</details>

stem_md: Find all complex numbers  $a,b,c\in\mathbb{C}^*$  such that   $$ |a\overline{b}+b\overline{c}+c\overline{a}|=|a|^2+|b|^2+|c|^2. $$  *Mihai Opincariu*
solution_md:
By Triangle Inequality we have
    \[
        |a\bar{b}|+|b\bar{c}|+|c\bar{a}|\geq|a\bar{b}+b\bar{c}+c\bar{a}|=|a|^2+|b|^2+|c|^2
    \]
    Since  $|\bar{z}|=|z|$ , we therefore obtain:
    \begin{align*}
        |a||b|+|b||c|+|c||a|\geq|a|^2+|b|^2+|c|^2
        2|a|^2+2|b|^2+2|c|^2-2|a||b|-2|b||c|-2|c||a|\leq0
        (|a|-|b|)^2+(|b|-|c|)^2+(|c|-|a|)^2 \leq0
    \end{align*}
    Thus,  $|a|=|b|=|c|$ . We now prove  $a=b=c$ . Using  $z\cdot\bar{z}=|z|^2$  we have
    \begin{align*}
        |a\bar{b}+b\bar{c}+c\bar{a}|&=|a|^2+|b|^2+|c|^2
        \Bigg|\frac{a|a|^2}{b}+\frac{b|a|^2}{c}+\frac{c|a|^2}{a}\Bigg|&=3|a|^2
        \Bigg|\frac{a}{b}+\frac{b}{c}+\frac{c}{a}\Bigg|&=3
    \end{align*}
    Applying Triangle Inequality again we have:
    \[
        \Bigg|\frac{a}{b}\Bigg|+\Bigg|\frac{b}{c}\Bigg|+\Bigg|\frac{c}{a}\Bigg|\geq3
    \]
    But, since  $|a|=|b|=|c|$ , we get:
    \[
        \Bigg|\frac{a}{b}\Bigg|+\Bigg|\frac{b}{c}\Bigg|+\Bigg|\frac{c}{a}\Bigg|=1+1+1=3
    \]
    Therefore, we obtain equality in Triangle Inequality so, since  $a,b,c\neq0$ ,   $$ \frac{a}{b}=\frac{b}{c}=\frac{c}{a}=\frac{a+b+c}{b+c+a}=1 $$   Hence  $\boxed{a=b=c}$ .

stem_md: Find all continuous functions  $f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$  such that  $f(x+y)=f(x+f(y))$  for all  $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$ .
solution_md:
Very beautiful!  $f(x) = x$  is good.

Assume there exists  $c \in \mathbb{R}$  such that  $f(c) \neq c$ , say  $f(c) > c$ . (*)

The hypothesis can be rewritten as  $f(x) = f(x + g(y))$ ,  $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ , where  $g \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ ,  $g(y) = f(y) - y$ .

As  $f$  is continuous,  $g$  is continuous as well, and by (*) we get that either  $g$  is constant (which easily gives  $f(x)=x$ , false) or there exist  $T_2>T_1>0$  such that  $[T_1, T_2] \subset \text{Im}\ g$ . Notice that any number in  $\text{Im}\ g$  is a period of  $f$  (again, by (*)). We will now prove that  $f$  is constant. 

For doing so, we will show that  $\forall r \in \mathbb{R}, \exists x_r, y_r \in \text{Im}\ g, \alpha_r, \beta_r \in \mathbb{Z}$  such that
\[
r = x_r \alpha_r + y_r \beta_r 
\]
This could be rewritten as (dividing by, say,  $\alpha_r$ ; if  $\alpha_r=0$  we divide by  $\beta_r$ , and if  $\beta_r=0$  as well then  $r=0$  and this is of no interest) \[ \exists \gamma_r \in \mathbb{Q}, \exists x_r, y_r \in \text{Im}\ g \text{ such that } r = x_r+ y_r \gamma_r, \]
Let  $y_r \in [T_1, T_2] \subset \text{Im}\ g$  be arbitrary.

It suffices to find a  $\gamma_r \in \mathbb{Q}$  such that
\[
T_1 \leq r - y_r \gamma_r \le T_2
\]

But this can be rewritten as  $\exists \gamma_r \in \mathbb{Q}  \text{ such that } \frac{r-T_2}{y_r} \leq \gamma_r \leq  \frac{r-T_1}{y_r}$ , which is obviously true as  $\mathbb{Q}$  is dense in  $\mathbb{R}$ .


Let  $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$  be arbitrary with  $x<y$ . By the above, there exist  $x_0, y_0 \in \text{Im}\ g, \alpha_0, \beta_0 \in \mathbb{Z}$  such that
\[
y - x = x_0 \alpha_0 + y_0 \beta_0
\]

Thus  $f(y) = f(x + (y - x)) = f(x + x_0 \alpha_0 + y_0 \beta_0) \overset{(*)}{=} f(x)$ , and so  $f$  is constant.

stem_md:
Let  $n\geq 2$  and  $A,B\in\mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{C})$  such that   $$ \{\text{rank}(A^k)\mid k\geq 1\}=\{\text{rank}(B^k)\mid k\geq 1\}. $$   Prove that  $\text{rank}(A^k)=\text{rank}(B^k)$  for all  $k\geq 1$ .

*Cristi Săvescu*
solution_md:
Very cute problem.

For any matrix  $J \in \mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{C})$  the sequence  $\left(\text{rank}(J^k)\right)_{k \geq 1}$  is strictly decreasing up to an index, then constant. This can be easily proved using the Jordan form of  $J$ , or even in an elementary way, by Frobenius. From now I will use  $R_J$  for the set  $\{\text{rank}(J^k)\mid k\geq 1\}$ .

Now we basically only need to observe two things: 

The first thing is: say  $k_A, k_B$  are those indices from where the rank-sequence of  $A$ , respectively  $B$ , get constant. Then  $k_A=k_B$  and  $\text{rank}(A^{k_A})=\text{rank}(B^{k_B})$ . The first part is because  $|R_A|=k_A$  and  $|R_B|=k_B$ . The second part is because  $\text{rank}(A^{k_A})$  and  $\text{rank}(B^{k_B})$  are the smallest terms in the sets  $R_A$  and  $R_B$ , respectively.

The second thing is to just observe the following equality of sets:  $\{\text{rank}(A^1) > \text{rank}(A^2) > \ldots > \text{rank}(A^{k})\}=\{\text{rank}(B^1) > \text{rank}(B^2) > \ldots > \text{rank}(B^{k})\}$ , where  $k=k_A=k_B$ . The result is now clear; just match the terms from biggest to smallest (one can even do this by induction, but even that would be kind of an overkill, as the number of steps we have to do is finite).

candidates:
If a₀ = 1: 
a₁ = (1² − 1)/1 = 0 
a₂ = (0² − 1)/2 = −1/2

So 1 is a threshold.

If a₀ > 1:
Then aₙ² − 1 > 0, and each term is positive.
As n increases, the denominator grows slowly, but the numerator grows faster (quadratically).
So aₙ increases and eventually diverges to infinity.

If a₀ ∈ [0, 1): Then aₙ² − 1 < 0, so each next term is negative or decreasing. Sequence tends toward zero.

Conclusion: 
a = 1 is the threshold.
If a₀ ≥ 1, then aₙ -> ∞.
If a₀ < 1, then aₙ -> 0.

stem_md:
Let  $G$  be a finite group and  $a\in G$  a fixed element. Define the set   $$ S_a=\{g\in G\mid ga\neq ag, \,ga^2=a^2g\}. $$   Show that:
[list=a]
[*] if  $g\in S_a$ , then  $ag^{-1}\in S_a$ ;
[*]  $|S_a|$  is divisible by  $4$ .
solution_md:
(1): If  $g \in S_a$ , then  $g^-1 \in S_a$ .
Demo:  $ga 
eq ag \Rightarrow g^-1ga 
eq g^-1ag \Rightarrow a 
eq g^-1ag \Rightarrow a(g^-1)

stem_md: Let  $f:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$  be a continuous function. Prove that   $$ \int_0^{\pi/2}f(\sin(2x))\sin x\, dx = \int_0^{\pi/2} f(\cos^2 x)\cos x\, dx. $$
solution_md:
Note that   $$ I=\int_0^{\pi/2} f(\sin 2x)\cos x dx
=\int_0^{\pi/2} f(\sin 2x)\sin xdx. $$  \begin{align*}
2I
&=\int_0^{\pi/2}f(\sin 2x)(\cos x+\sin x)dx
&=\int_0^{\pi/2}f(1-(\sin x-\cos x)^2)d(\sin x-\cos x).
&=\int_{-1}^1f(1-u^2)du
&=2\int_0^1f(1-u^2)du
&=2\int_0^{\pi/2}f\left(\cos^2(t)\right)\cos(t)dt.
\end{align*}

stem_md: Let  $\mathcal{P}_n$  be the set of all real monic polynomial functions of degree  $n$ . Prove that for any  $a<b$ ,   $$ \inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}_n}\int_a^b |P(x)|\, dx >0. $$  *Cristi Săvescu*
solution_md:
Let  $V$  be the linear space spanned by  $1,\cdots,x^{n-1}$  then we want to show that  $d(x^n,V)>0$  in  $L^1[a,b]$ .
Now  $V$  is a finite dimensional subspace of a Banach space, hence closed. This uses the fact that all norms on a finite dimensional space are equivalent. 
Hence  $d(x^n,V)=0$  would imply  $x^n\in V$  which is a contradiction.
Indeed,  $x^n=\sum_0^{n-1}a _k x^k$  in  $L^1$  would imply  $x^n=\sum_0^{n-1} a_kx^k$  for all  $x\in [0,1]$  since the functions are continuous. Then the difference polynomial has inf many roots, contradiction.

stem_md:
Let  $R$  be a ring. Let  $x,y\in R$  such that  $x^2=y^2=0$ . Prove that if  $x+y-xy$  is nilpotent, so is  $xy$ .

*Janez Šter*
solution_md:
Let \((x+y-xy)^k=0, k\in\mathbb{N}\), where \(k\) is the degree. If \(k=1:x(x+y-xy)=0\xRightarrow{\hspace{25pt}}\boxed{xy=0}.\)
If \(k\geqslant 2: x(x+y-xy)^k=xy(x+y-xy)^{k-1}=0=(x+y-xy)^k\xRightarrow{\hspace{25pt}}(x+y)(x+y-xy)^{k-1}=0.\)
\(\xRightarrow{\hspace{25pt}}yx(x+y-xy)^{k-1}=0\xRightarrow{\hspace{25pt}}(xy)^2(x+y-xy)^{k-2}=0.\)
Now suppose we have proven \((xy)^a(x+y-xy)^{k-a}=0\quad \forall 1\le a\le n\). We will prove it for \(n+1\).
[asy]usepackage("amsmath, amssymb, tikz, tikz-cd");
label("\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
\scriptstyle(xy)^n(x+y-xy)^{k-n}+(xy)^{n-1}(x+y-xy)^{k-n+1}=0\&\&\scriptstyle(xy)^{n-1}(x+y)(x+y-xy)^{k-n}=0.
\arrow[Rightarrow, from=1-1, to=1-3]
\end{tikzcd}");[/asy]
So [asy]usepackage("amsmath, amssymb, tikz, tikz-cd");
label("\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
\scriptstyle(xy)^{n-1}xyx(x+y-xy)^{k-n}=0\&\&\scriptstyle(xy)^{n+1}(x+y-xy)^{k-n-1}=0.
\arrow[Rightarrow, from=1-1, to=1-3]
\end{tikzcd}");[/asy]
Hence [asy]usepackage("amsmath, amssymb, tikz, tikz-cd");
label("\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
\hspace{1pt}\&\&\color{blue}\scriptstyle \exists k\in\mathbb{N}\ (xy)^k=0.
\arrow[Rightarrow, blue, from=1-1, to=1-3]
\end{tikzcd}");[/asy]

Let x and y be elements in a ring such that x squared = 0 and y squared = 0.
Suppose a = x + y - xy is nilpotent.

When you expand powers of a, like a squared, you get terms like xy, yx, and (xy)^2.
Because x squared and y squared are zero, many terms drop out.
This means that powers of a eventually involve powers of xy.

Since a to some power is zero, and that includes powers of xy,
it must be that some power of xy is also zero.

Therefore, xy is nilpotent.

stem_md: Prove that for any given number  $a_k, 1 \le k \le 5$ , there are  $\lambda_k \in \{-1, 0, 1\}, 1 \le k \le 5$ , which are not all equal zero, such that  $11 | \lambda_1a_1^2+\lambda_2a_2^2+\lambda_3a_3^2+\lambda_4a_4^2+\lambda_5a_5^2$
solution_md:
It seems that we can replace  $11$  with any positive integer  $n$  less than  $32$ .

To see this, fix a  $\Lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_5)\in\{0,1\}^5$ , and let  $S_\Lambda = \sum_{i=1}^5 \lambda_i a_i^2$ . Since the set of all such  $\Lambda$ 's has  $32$  elements, and  $n<32$ , there exists  $\Lambda'\neq \Lambda''$ , such that  $S_{\Lambda'}\equiv S_{\Lambda''}\pmod{n}$ . It then follows that,  $\sum_{i=1}^5 (\lambda_i'-\lambda_i'')a_i^2\equiv 0\pmod{n}$ . Letting  $\lambda_i = \lambda'_i-\lambda''_i$ , we see that  $(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_i)\neq (0,0,0,0,0)$ ; and  $\lambda_i\in\{-1,0,1\}$ , as desired.

stem_md:
Let   $(f_n) _{n\ge 0}$  be the sequence defined by $ f_0 = 0, f_1 = 1, f_{n + 2 }= f_{n + 1} + f_n$  for  $n> 0$  (Fibonacci string) 
and let   $t_n =$   ${n+1}\choose{2}$   for  $n \ge 1$  . Prove that:
a)  $f_1^2+f_2^2+...+f_n^2 = f_n \cdot f_{n+1}$  for  $n \ge 1$ b)  $\frac{1}{n^2} \cdot \Sigma_{k=1}^{n}\left( \frac{t_k}{f_k}\right)^2 \ge \frac{t_{n+1}^2}{9 f_n \cdot f_{n+1}}$
solution_md: Here we go. $a)$  We induct on  $n$ . Base cases are easy. Now, suppose the statement is true for  $n-1$ , that is,  $f_1^2+\cdots+f_{n-1}^2 =f_{n-1}f_n$ . Now,   $f_1^2+\cdots+f_n^2 = f_n^2+f_{n-1}f_n = f_n(f_{n-1}+f_n)=f_n f_{n+1}$ , using Fibonacci recursion, completing the induction.  $b)$  Using part  $(a)$  we replace  $f_nf_{n+1}$  by  $\Sigma_{k=1}^n f_k^2$ . Now, using Cauchy-Schwarz:  $$ \left(\sum_{k=1}^n f_k^2\right)\left(\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{t_k^2}{f_k^2}\right)\geq \left(\sum_{k=1}^n t_k\right)^2. $$  Thus, it suffices to show,   $$ \frac{t_1+\cdots+t_n}{n}\geq \frac13 t_{n+1}. $$  However, using  $t_i = \frac{k(k+1)}{2}$ , we obtain immediately that  $\frac{t_1+\cdots+t_n}{n}=\frac13 t_{n+1}$ , thus we are done.

stem_md: Let  $ x,y$  be reals s.t.  $ x^2\plus{}y^2\leq1$  and  $ n$  a natural number.Prove that: $ (x^n\plus{}y)^2\plus{}y^2\geq\dfrac{1}{n\plus{}2}(x^2\plus{}y^2)^n$
solution_md:
Let $ x,y$ be reals s.t. $ x^2\plus{}y^2\leq1$ and $ n$ a natural number.Prove that: $ (x^n\plus{}y)^2\plus{}y^2\geq\dfrac{1}{n\plus{}2}(x^2\plus{}y^2)^n$
Using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have \[(x^n+y)^2+\frac{2}{n+2}y^2 \ge \frac{(x^n+y-y)^2}{1+\frac{n+2}{2}}=\frac{2}{n+4}x^{2n}.\] Therefore, \[\begin{aligned} (x^n+y)^2+y^2&=\left[(x^n+y)^2+\frac{2}{n+2}y^2\right] +\frac{n}{n+2}y^2 \ge \frac{2}{n+4}x^{2n}+\frac{n}{n+2}y^2 &\ge \frac{2}{n+4}x^{2n}+\frac{n}{n+2} y^2(x^2+y^2)^{n-1}. \end{aligned}\] It suffices to proe that \[\frac{2}{n+4}x^{2n}+\frac{n}{n+2}y^2(x^2+y^2)^{n-1} \ge \frac{1}{n+2}(x^2+y^2)^2,\] or \[\frac{2n+4}{n+4}x^{2n} \ge (x^2+y^2)^{n-1} \big[x^2-(n-1)y^2\big].\] If $x^2 \le (n-1)y^2,$ then the inequality is obviously true. Otherwise, using the AM-GM inequality, we have \[\begin{aligned} (x^2+y^2)^{n-1}\big[x^2-(n-1)y^2\big] &\le \left[\frac{(n-1)(x^2+y^2)+x^2-(n-1)y^2}{n}\right]^n &=x^{2n} \le \frac{2n+4}{n+4} x^{2n}.\end{aligned}\] This ends our proof.

stem_md: Find all prime numbers  $ p $  for which  $ 1 + p\cdot 2^{p} $  is a perfect square.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>The answer is  $p=2$  and  $p=3$  only, leading to the perfect squares  $9$  and  $25$ .

Now suppose that  $p\ge 5$  and that  $1 +p\cdot 2^p = x^2$  for a positive integer  $x$ . Then  $(x+1)(x-1) = p\cdot 2^p$ , and as both  $x+1$ ,  $x-1$  must be even, we also have that  $\frac{x+1}{2}\cdot \frac{x-1}{2} = p\cdot 2^{p-2}$ . As  $\gcd\left(\frac{x+1}{2},\frac{x-1}{2}\right) = 1$ , we require  $|2^{p-2} - p| = 1$ . However, for  $p=5$ ,  $2^{3}> 5+1$ , and it is clear that  $2^{p-2}>p+1$  for all positive integers  $p\ge 5$ , a contradiction. Hence, there are no solutions  $p\ge 5$ .</details>

solution_md:

Proof of Zhangyanzong: When $\sin^{2}x\cos^{2}x=0,$ $$ \sqrt {\frac {\sin^{2}x}{1 + \cos^{2}x}} + \sqrt {\frac {\cos^{2}x}{1 + \sin^{2}x}}= 1 ; $$ When $\sin^{2}x\cos^{2}x\neq 0,$ $$ \sqrt {\frac {\sin^{2}x}{1 + \cos^{2}x}} + \sqrt {\frac {\cos^{2}x}{1 + \sin^{2}x}}=\frac {\sin^{2}x}{\sqrt {sin^2x (1 + \cos^{2}x)}} + \frac {\cos^{2}x}{\sqrt {cos^2x(1 + \sin^{2}x)}}>\frac {\sin^{2}x}{\frac {sin^2x+ (1 + \cos^{2}x)}{2}}+ \frac {\cos^{2}x}{\frac {cos^2x+(1 + \sin^{2}x)}{2}}=1. $$

stem_md: The diagonals of the cyclic quadrilateral  $ ABCD$  are intersecting at the point  $ E$ . $ K$  and  $ M$  are the midpoints of  $ AB$  and  $ CD$ , respectively. Let the points  $ L$  on  $ BC$  and  $ N$  on  $ AD$  s.t. $ EL\perp BC$  and  $ EN\perp AD$ .Prove that  $ KM\perp LN$ .
solution_md:
The diagonals of the cyclic quadrilateral $ ABCD$ are intersecting at the point $ E$ . $ K$ and $ M$ are the midpoints of $ AB$ and $ CD$ , respectively. Let the points $ L$ on $ BC$ and $ N$ on $ AD$ s.t. $ EL\perp BC$ and $ EN\perp AD$ .Prove that $ KM\perp LN$ .
SolutionLet $ P$ be the intersection between $ AD$ and $ BC$ , let $ Y$ and $ X$ be the respective orthocenters of $ \triangle PAC$ and $ \triangle PBD$ , let $ YA$ and $ PC$ meet at $ Q$ , let $ YC$ meet $ PD$ at $ R$ , and let the intersections between $ PY$ and $ AC$ and $ PX$ and $ BD$ be $ T$ and $ U$ respectively. Now, since $ ABCD$ is cyclic, we have that $ \triangle PBD\sim \triangle PAC$ , so $ \frac {PT}{PY} \equal{} \frac {PU}{PX}$ , so $ TU\parallel XY$ . Furthermore, $ (TU, PD) \equal{} \angle TPN \plus{} \angle PTU$ . Since $ \angle ENP \equal{} 90 \equal{} \angle PLE \equal{} \angle PUE \equal{} \angle ETP$ (notice that since $ Y$ is the orthocenter of $ \triangle PAC$ , we have that $ CT\perp PY$ , and similarly, $ DU\perp PX$ ), we have that $ ENTPUL$ is cyclic, so $ (TU, PD) \equal{} \angle AEN \plus{} \angle PEB$ from $ \angle AEN \equal{} \angle APT$ and $ \angle PTU \equal{} \angle PEB$ . Then, $ Q$ lies on the circle with diameter $ AB$ and $ R$ lies on that with diameter $ CD$ . Since $ \angle ARC \plus{} \angle AQC \equal{} 90 \plus{} 90 \equal{} 180$ , we have that $ AQCR$ is cyclic, so $ YA\cdot YQ \equal{} YR\cdot YC$ . stem_md: Let  $a,b,c$  be real numbers with sum equal to zero. Prove that \[ab^3+bc^3+ca^3\leqslant 0.\]
solution_md: By Rearrangement Inequality we have  $a^4+b^4+c^4 \geqslant |b^3c| + |c^3a| + |a^3b| \geqslant -b^3c  -c^3a  -a^3b$ , so  $ ab^3+bc^3+ca^3 = \sum_{cyc} (-b-c)b^3 \leqslant 0$   $\blacksquare$ .

stem_md: At a company, there are several workers, some of which are enemies. They go to their job with 100 buses, in such a way that there aren't any enemies in either bus. Having arrived at the job, their chief wants to assign them to brigades of at least two people, without assigning two enemies to the same brigade. Prove that the chief can split the workers in at most 100 brigades, or he cannot split them at all in any number of brigades.
solution_md:
Let's formulate in graph theory
We have  $k$  disjoint cliques and prove that either we cannot partition the vertices in  $k$  cliques with lenght $\ge 2$  or if we can, we can do in at most k cliques
Let  $v_1,..,v_t$  the singletons;  $(x_1,y_1);...; (x_l,y_l)$  the cliques with lenght 2 and  $C_1,..,C_m$  the ones with lenght $\ge 3$ Some observations:
1)Obviously  $v_i$  and  $v_j$  cannot be adiacent otherwise we decrease t
2)  $v_1$  cannot be adiacent with some  $u\in C_j$  as otherwise we can put  $v_1$  and  $u$  in same clique and decrease  $t$ 3)we cannot have  $v_1,x_1$  adiacent and  $v_2,y_1$  as otherwise we do 2 groups and  $t\rightarrow t-2$ So suppose we have the groups. Then  $v_1,..,v_t$  are in different groups with(WLOG)  $x_1,..,x_t$  and now  $y_1,..,y_t$  are singletons which forces again observations 1),2),3) but this time for  $y_1,..,y_t$ .One more observation is that  $y_i$  cannot be in the first t groups otherwise we decrease t
so again this should create other t groups with $ x_{t+1},..,x_{2t}$  and this gives  $l\ge 2t$ .
By same reasoning  $l\ge nt$  for every  $n \in \mathbb N$  which is false
So we decrease t and we can do induction because the total number of groups didn't increase  during the process and so we can do at most number of groups $\le k $  or we can't so we can't also in the original one.

Suppose there exists an arbitrary partition  $\mathcal{P}_1$  of the workers in brigades. We will creater the desired partition  $\mathcal{P}_2$  into  $k\leqslant 100$  brigades algorithmically. Initially we form the (possibly empty) groups  $G_1,\ldots,G_{100}$  where  $G_i$  consists of the people in bus number  $i.{}$  If all the groups has zero or at least two members, they are all brigades and we found the partition  $\mathcal{P}_2$ .

Othewise, choose a group  $G_k$  with exactly one member  $m{}.$  We perform the following operation: extract the workers which are in the same brigade with  $m{}$  in  $\mathcal{P}_1$  from their current groups and place them in  $G_k.$  Then, continue the process with some other group with one person, or otherwise stop.

The key observation is that once we have performed an operation on a group  $G_k$ , it has at least two members and no enemies and we will never alter its members again, as they are all members of one brigade in  $\mathcal{P}_1.$  Therefore, when the process stops, we get the desired partition  $\mathcal{P}_2.$

stem_md:
Does there exist an increasing sequence of positive integers for which any large enough integer can be expressed uniquely as the sum of two (possibly equal) terms of the sequence?

*Proposed by Vlad Spătaru and David Anghel*
solution_md:
Apparently, there is a beautiful generalisation to this problem, due to Donald J. Newman. The proof we present is taken from *Straight From The Book*, by T. Andreescu and G. Dospinescu. Here is the statement:**Generalisation.** Let  $\mathcal{A}$  be an infinite set of positive integers. Let  $x_n$  be the number of pairs  $(a,b)$  of elements of  $\mathcal{A}$  such that  $a<b$  and  $a+b=n.$  Prove that the sequence  $(x_n)_{n\geqslant 1}$  is not eventually constant.**Solution.** Consider the generating function \[f(x)=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}} x^a.\]Note that  $f(z)$  converges for all  $|z|<1$  and that  $z\mapsto f(z)$  is a continuous function on the open unit disk. Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that the sequence  $(x_n)_{n\geqslant 1}$  is eventually constant. Then, \[f(X)^2-f(X^2)=\frac{c}{1-X}+P(x),\]for some constant  $c$  and polynomial  $P.$  We will prove that this cannot happen. The idea is to look at the behaviour of  $f{}$  on the real axis, close to 1 and then at its average behaviour on circles of radius tending to 1. We will write  $f\gg g$  when  $f$  and  $g$  are positive functions on  $(0,1)$  if there exists a constant  $c>0$  such that  $f(r)>cg(r)$  in a neighbourhood of 1.

In particular, observe that  $|P|\ll 1$  and because  $f(x^2)>0$  for  $x\in(0,1)$  then  $f(x)\gg 1/\sqrt{1-x}.$  Now, we integrate the relation satisfies by  $f$  on circles of radius close to 1. Using the triangle inequality, we deduce that for all  $r\in(0,1)$ \begin{align*}\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(re^{ix})|^2\mathrm{d}x\leqslant\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(r^2e^{ix})|\mathrm{d}x+\sup_{|z|\leqslant 1}|P(z)|+\frac{c}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{|1-re^{ix}|}.\end{align*}For the sake of brevity, let the last summand in the right-hand side be  $cF(r).$  Using Parseval's identity, we obtain\[\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(re^{ix})|^2\mathrm{d}x=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}r^{2a}=f(r^2).\]On the other hand, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and Parseval's identity yield\[\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(r^2e^{ix})|\mathrm{d}x\leqslant\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(r^2e^{ix})|^2\mathrm{d}x}=\sqrt{f(r^4)}\leqslant\sqrt{f(r^2)}.\]Putting these remarks togheter, we obtain the estimate  $f(r^2)\leqslant\sqrt{f(r^2)}+C_1+C_2F(r)$  for some constants  $C_1,C_2>0.$  

This immediately yields  $f(r^2)\ll 1+F(r).$  By also using  $f(x)\gg 1/\sqrt{1-x}$  we deduce that  $1+F(r)\gg1/\sqrt{1-r^2}.$  Thus, it remains to prove that this cannot happen. Note that for  $0\leqslant x\leqslant\pi$  we have\[|1-re^{ix}|^2=(1-r)^2+4r\sin^2(x/2)\geqslant (1-r)^2+4rx^2/\pi^2.\]Therefore, we have\begin{align*}F(r)=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^\pi\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{|1-re^{ix}|}\leqslant\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^\pi\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\sqrt{(1-r)^2+4rx^2/\pi^2}}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{r}}\text{arcsinh}\left(\frac{2\sqrt{r}}{1-r}\right).\end{align*}It follows that\[\lim_{r\to 1^-}\frac{F(r)}{-\ln(1-r)}\leqslant\frac{1}{2}\implies\lim_{r\to1^-}\sqrt{1-r}F(r)=0.\]Naturally, this contradicts  $1+F(r)\gg1/\sqrt{1-r^2}$  as desired.  $\square$

The answer is negative. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that such a sequence  $a_1,a_2,\ldots$  exists. Then, any  $n>n_0$  may be written uniequely as  $a_i+a_j.$  Choose some  $T$  for which all  $a_i$  with  $i\geqslant T$  exceed  $n_0.$  For every  $i,j\geqslant T$  the sums  $a_i+a_j$  are greater than  $n_0$  so they are pairwise distinct. Thus, the differences  $a_i-a_j$  for  $i,j\geqslant T$  are also pairwise distinct.

For the sake of simplicity, we will decrease the indices of the sequence by  $T$  as seen below \[a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots\mapsto a_{1-T},\ldots,a_{-1},a_0,a_1,\ldots.\]Hence, the differences  $a_i-a_j$  with  $i,j>0$  are pairwise distinct. We will estimate how many terms  $a_k$  of the sequence can be smaller than some arbitrary (and large) positive integer  $N.$  Assume that  $a_n<N$  and fix some positive integer  $\Delta<n.$  Then \[\frac{\#_p^2}{2}<\sum_{k=1}^{\#_p}k\leqslant\sum_{k=1}^\Delta\sum_{\substack{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant n  j-i=k}}(a_j-a_i)\leqslant \sum_{k=1}^\Delta kN=N\cdot \frac{\Delta(\Delta+1)}{2},\]where  $\#_p$  is the number of pairs of indices  $2\leqslant i,j\leqslant n$  for which  $1\leqslant j-i\leqslant\Delta$ . One may see that  $\#_p\geqslant \Delta(n-\Delta)$  so substituing in the previous estimate we get \[n\leqslant\Delta+\sqrt{N+\frac{N}{\Delta}}.\]Therefore, we either have  $n\leqslant N^{1/3}$  or we can substitute  $\Delta=\lfloor N^{1/3}\rfloor$  in the previous estimate for  $n.{}$  Either way we get that  $n\leqslant \sqrt{N}(1+\varepsilon_N)$  where  $\varepsilon_N$  is an error term which tends to  $0$  as  $N{}$  tends to infinity. 

Therefore, there are at most  $f(N):=T+\sqrt{N}(1+\varepsilon_N)$  tends of the sequence not exceeding  $N.$  Consequently, the number of sums  $a_i+a_j$  that do not exceed  $N{}$  is at most \[\binom{f(N)}{2}+f(N)=N\cdot\frac{(1+\varepsilon_N)^2}{2}+\sqrt{N}\cdot\frac{3(1+\varepsilon_N)}{2}+C,\]where  $C$  is some constant. Recall, however, that any  $n>n_0$  can be expressed as  $a_i+a_j$  hence the above quantity must be at greater than or equal to  $N-n_0$ . This is a contradiction if  $N$  is chosen to be large enough.

<details><summary>solution</summary>Suppose for the sake of contradiction that such a sequence exists. Let  $a_1, a_2, \dots$  denote the increasing sequence. Consider the generating function \[f(X) = x^{a_1}+x^{a_2}+\dots\]
The generating function  $g$  counting the number of ways a nonnegative integer  $m$  can be expressed as  $a_i+a_j$  for some  $1 \leq i \leq j$  is given by \[g(X) = \frac{1}{2}[f(X)^2+f(X^2)]\]
(a direct product would have failed since it would have counted expressing  $a_i+a_j$  and  $a_j+a_i~$  twice, rather than the single representation it should contribute)

On the other hand, since the number of ways such a representation can be done is  $1$  for large enough  $n$ , it follows that there exists some (finite) polynomial  $P$  with \[g(X) = P(X)+x^N+x^{N+1}+\dots\]
It follows that there exists some polynomial  $Q$  such that \[f(X)^2+f(X^2) = Q(X)+\frac{2}{1-X}\]
Note that the above generating functions converge in the interval  $x \in (-1, 1)$ . Since  $f(x)^2 \geq 0$  for all  $|x| < 1$ , we obtain that \[Q(X)+\frac{2}{1-X} \geq f(X^2)\] for all  $|x| < 1$ .
But now note that while the left hand side in the above expression has a limit as  $x \mapsto -1^{+}$  the right hand diverges. (to positive  $\infty$  too, since all the summands of  $f(x^2)$  themselves are squares, thus nonnegative).  

This is a contradiction and thus there is no such sequence  $\{a_n\}_{n \geq 1}$ .  $\square$</details>

stem_md: Prove that if  $N{}$  is a large enough positive integer, then for any permutation  $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_N$  of  $1,\ldots, N$  at least  $11\%$  of the pairs  $(i,j)$  of indices from  $1{}$  to  $N{}$  satisfy  $\gcd(i,j)=1=\gcd(\pi_i,\pi_j).$ *Proposed by Vlad Spătaru*
solution_md: Consider a graph on the vertices  $v_1,\ldots,v_N$ . Draw a red edge between some vertices  $v_i{}$  and  $v_j{}$  if  $\gcd(i,j)=1$  and a blue one if  $\gcd(\pi_i,\pi_j)=1$ . We want to show that if  $N$  is large enough, then at least  $11\%$  of the pairs of vertices have edges of both colors. Letting  $E_r$  and  $E_b$  be the number of red and blue edges, respectively, it suffices to show that \[E_r+E_b\geqslant\binom{N}{2}\left(1+\frac{11}{100}\right).\]Since  $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_N$  is a permutation of  $1,\ldots,n$  then  $E_r=E_b$ . Furthermore, one may easily see that \[E_a=E_r=\Phi(N):=\sum_{k=1}^N\varphi(k).\]Therefore, the problem boils down to estimating  $\Phi(N)$ . We start with the well-known fact that  $n$  is the sum of the Euler totient function computed at its positive divisors. Applying Mobius inversion on this identity, we get \begin{align*}\Phi(N)&=\sum_{k=1}^N\varphi(k)=\sum_{k=1}^N\sum_{d\mid k}\mu(d)\cdot\frac{k}{d}=\sum_{k=1}^Nk\sum_{d\mid k}\frac{\mu(d)}{d}  &=\sum_{d=1}^N\frac{\mu(d)}{d}\sum_{\substack{k=1  d\mid k}}^Nk=\sum_{d=1}^N\mu(d)\sum_{l=1}^{\lfloor N/d\rfloor}l=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{d=1}^N\mu(d)\left\lfloor\frac{N}{d}\right\rfloor\left(\left\lfloor\frac{N}{d}\right\rfloor+1\right).\end{align*}Using the inequality for the floor function  $x\geqslant\lfloor x\rfloor>x-1$  and the fact that  $\mu$  only takes the values  $0,\pm 1$  we get\[\mu(d)\left\lfloor\frac{N}{d}\right\rfloor\left(\left\lfloor\frac{N}{d}\right\rfloor+1\right)\geqslant\mu(d)\left(\frac{N}{d}\right)^2-\frac{N}{d},\]hence substituting in the previous formula for  $\Phi(N)$  it follows that \[\Phi(N)\geqslant \frac{1}{2}\sum_{d=1}^N\left(\mu(d)\left(\frac{N}{d}\right)^2-\frac{N}{d}\right)=\frac{N^2}{2}\sum_{d=1}^N\frac{\mu(d)}{d^2}-\frac{N}{2}\sum_{d=1}^N\frac{1}{d}.\]We will estimate each of the two sums in the previous eastimate separately. Starting with the first one, simply notice that \begin{align*}\frac{N^2}{2}\sum_{d=1}^N\frac{\mu(d)}{d^2}&=\frac{N^2}{2}\left(\sum_{d=1}^{\infty}\frac{\mu(d)}{d^2}-\sum_{d>N}\frac{\mu(d)}{d^2}\right)\geqslant\frac{N^2}{2}\prod_{p\text{ prime}}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^2}\right)-\frac{N^2}{2}\sum_{d>N}\frac{1}{d^2}  &\geqslant \frac{N^2}{2}\prod_{p\text{ prime}}\left(\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{1}{p^{2k}}\right)^{-1}-\frac{N^2}{2}\sum_{d>N}\frac{1}{d(d-1)}=\frac{N^2}{2\zeta(2)}-\frac{N}{2}.\end{align*}The second sum is the  $N$ -th harmonic number, times  $N/2$ . It is well-known (and elementary) that  $H_N\leqslant\log_2 N+1$  so I'll omit the details. Using this and the previous inequality in the estimate for  $\Phi(N)$  we further get \[\Phi(N)\geqslant\frac{N^2}{2\zeta(2)}-\left(N+\frac{N\log_2 N}{2}\right).\]Showing that our initial inequality holds for all large enough  $N$  is now a matter of showing that  $2/\zeta(2)\geqslant 1+11/100$  which can be done by telescoping the terms  $1/i^2$  for  $i\geqslant 3$  and we're done.

stem_md:
Find all positive integers  $n\geqslant 2$  such that  $d_{i+1}/d_i$  is an integer for all  $1\leqslant i < k$ , where  $1=d_1<d_2<\dots <d_k=n$  are all the positive divisors of  $n$ .

*Proposed by Pavel Ciurea*
solution_md:
We claim that  $n$  is a prime power, which of course works as  $\frac{p^{i+1}}{p^i}$  is always an integer. Now we prove that numbers with at least two distinct prime factors fail.
Note that the condition is equivalent to  $d_i \mid d_j$  for all  $1 \le i < j \le k$ . Consider any two prime divisors  $p, q$  of  $n$ . Let  $p = d_a, q = d_b$ , and WLOG  $p > q \implies a > b$ . Then  $q \mid p$ , contradiction as  $p$  and  $q$  are distinct primes.  $\square$

stem_md:
On the screen of a computer there is an  $2^n\times 2^n$  board. On each cell of the main diagonal there is a file. At each step, we may select some files and move them to the left, on their respective rows, by the same distance. What is the minimum number of necessary moves in order to put all files on the first column?

*Proposed by Vlad Spătaru*
solution_md: Without loss of generality, assume that the minimum moves in order are moving by distances  $a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_m$  of some files. Each number from 1 to  $2^n - 1$  (corresponding to the distance of each file to the first column) is represented by the sum of some distinct move distances. From the above  $m$  moves, we can form at most  $2^m - 1$  distances. Hence  $2^m - 1 \geq 2^n - 1$ , or  $m \geq n$ . Equality happens for example when the moves are by distance  $1, 2, 2^2, ..., 2^{n-1}$  in order, and each file moves  $2^i$  steps when the representation in base 2 of its distance to the first column contains  $2^i$ .

stem_md: Let  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$  be positive real numbers such that  $a+b+c=3$ . Prove that   $$ \sqrt[3]{\frac{a^3+b^3}{2}}+\sqrt[3]{\frac{b^3+c^3}{2}}+\sqrt[3]{\frac{c^3+a^3}{2}}\leqslant a^2+b^2+c^2. $$  *Proposed by Andrei Vila*
solution_md:
Let $a$ , $b$ , $c$ be positive real numbers such that $a+b+c=3$ . Prove that $$ \sqrt[3]{\frac{a^3+b^3}{2}}+\sqrt[3]{\frac{b^3+c^3}{2}}+\sqrt[3]{\frac{c^3+a^3}{2}}\leqslant a^2+b^2+c^2. $$ *Proposed by Andrei Vila*
Using AM-GM and $a^2+b^2+c^2\geq 3$ : $$ \begin {aligned} \sum \sqrt[3]{\frac{a^3+b^3}{2}} &= \sum \sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{2}(a+b)(a^2-ab+b^2)} &\leq \frac{1}{3}\sum\left(1+\frac{a+b}{2}+a^2-ab+b^2\right) &= \frac{6+2(a^2+b^2+c^2)-ab-bc-ca}{3} &= \frac{3+5(a^2+b^2+c^2)}{6} &\leq a^2+b^2+c^2 \end{aligned} $$

stem_md:
Let  $n\geqslant 2$  be a fixed positive integer. Determine the minimum value of the expression   $$ \frac{a_{a_1}}{a_1}+\frac{a_{a_2}}{a_2}+\dots +\frac{a_{a_n}}{a_n}, $$   where  $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$  are positive integers at most  $n$ .

*Proposed by David Anghel*
solution_md:
Despite being easy, this problem has a very nice idea. I will sketch the solution. The answer is  $3-2/n$  which can be obtained by setting  $a_1=a_n=n$  and all the other  $a_i$  (if there are any) equal to one. The key idea is to consider an oriented graph on  $n$  vertices with the edges  $i\to a_i$ . Naturally, there exists at least one cycle in (every connected component of) this graph. 

If there exists a cycle of length  $\ell\geqslant 2$ , say  $v_1\to v_2\to\cdots\to v_\ell\to v_1$  then we have\[\sum_{i=1}^\ell\frac{a_{a_{v_i}}}{a_{v_i}}=\sum_{i=1}^\ell\frac{a_{v_{i+1}}}{a_{v_i}}\geqslant \ell\left(\prod_{i=1}^\ell\frac{a_{v_{i+1}}}{a_{v_i}}\right)^{1/\ell}=\ell.\]Additionally, all other ratios are greater than or equal to  $1/n$  so the expression is at least  $\ell+(n-\ell)/n\geqslant 3-2/n$ , as  $\ell\geqslant 2$ . If there are at least two cycles of lnegth one, say  $i\to i$  and  $j\to j$  then  $a_{a_i}/a_i+a_{a_j}/a_j=2$  and the remaining  $n-2$  ratios add up to at least  $(n-2)/n$  for a total of at least  $3-2/n$  so we are done.

Otherwise, the graph has precisely one cycle, which has length one. Let this cycle be  $i\to i$ . Moreover, it has only one connected component (in an undirected sense), so there exists  $j$  such that  $j\to i$ . Therefore  $a_{a_i}/a_i+a_{a_j}/a_j=2$  so we may finish the reasoning as outlined in the previous paragraph.

stem_md:
Consider the sequence  $a_1, a_2, \dots$  of positive integers such that  $a_1=2$  and  $a_{n+1}=a_n^4+a_n^3-3a_n^2-a_n+2$ , for all  $n\geqslant 1$ . Prove that there exist infinitely many prime numbers that don't divide any term of the sequence.

*Proposed by Pavel Ciurea*
solution_md:
One of the contestants had a remarkable idea, which I generalised to a larger class of polynomials.**General problem.** Let  $f\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$  be a polynomial with  $\deg f\geqslant 2$ . Define the sequence  $(a_i)_{i\geqslant 0}$  by  $a_0=0$  and  $a_{i+1}=f(a_i)$  for any  $i\geqslant 0$ . Prove that there exist infinitely many primes which do not divide any non-zero term of the sequence.**Solution.** If the sequence is bounded, then evidently any large enough prime number does not divide any of its non-zero terms. While this is a trivial observation, it will help us with the fluidity of the solution. We may thus rewrite the conclusion: prove that the sequence is bounded, or there exist infinitely many prime numbers which do not divide any of its on-zero terms.

Naturally, if  $f(0)=0$  then the sequence is bounded. Hence, let  $\lambda\neq 0$  be the constant term of  $f$ . By similar means, we may assume that  $f(\lambda)\neq\lambda$ . Write  $a_{i+1}=a_i\cdot g(a_i)+\lambda$  where  $g$  is a non-constant integral polynomial. Lastly, if some  $g(a_i)$  is zero, then the sequence is periodical so it is bounded. We assume that  $g(a_i)\neq 0$  for all  $i\geqslant 0$ . In particular,  $g(0)\neq 0$ .
 
Consider an arbitrary prime number  $p$ . Assume that some prime number  $q$  divides  $g(a_p)$ . Then,  $a_{p+1}\equiv\lambda\bmod{q}$ . However, by definition,  $a_1\equiv\lambda\bmod{q}$ . Hence, the sequence  $(a_i)_{i\geqslant 0}$  is periodical modulo  $q$  and the length  $\ell$  of the period divides  $p$ . If  $\ell=1$  then  $f(\lambda)\equiv\lambda\bmod{q}.$  Recall that  $f(\lambda)\neq\lambda$  so assume that  $q>|f(\lambda)-\lambda|$  to avoid this case.

Otherwise,  $\ell=p$  so the period modulo  $q$  is  $(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_p)$ . If we enforce  $q>|g(0)|$  further, since  $g(a_p)\equiv 0\bmod{q}$  we infer that  $a_p\not\equiv 0\bmod{q}$ , since  $g(0)\neq 0$ . Therefore, if there exists  $i$  such  $q\mid a_i$  then  $a_{i+1}\equiv\lambda\bmod{q}$  which is absurd, as this means  $0\to\lambda$  in our sequence (reduced modulo  $q$ ), whereas we've proven that  $a_p\to\lambda$  and  $a_p\not\equiv 0\bmod{q}$ .

Thus, if  $g(a_p)$  has a prime factor  $q$  greater than  $M:=\max(|f(\lambda)-\lambda|,|g(0)|)$  then  $q$  does not divide any non-zero term of the sequence and, addidtionally, the period modulo  $q{}$  is  $p{}$ . Consequently, it suffices to prove that there are infinitely many primes  $p{}$  for which  $g(a_p)$  has at least one prime factor greater than  $M{}.$ Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that this is not true. If  $g(\lambda)=0$  then the sequence is bounded, so we may assume that  $g(\lambda)\neq 0$ . Let  $i$  be an arbitrary integer and recall that  $g(a_i)
\neq 0$ . The main observation is that reducing the sequence modulo  $g(a_i)$  we have  $a_j\equiv\lambda\bmod{g(a_i)}$  hence  $g(a_j)\equiv g(\lambda)\bmod{g(a_i})$  for any  $j\equiv 1\bmod{i}$ .

We split the prime numbers not exceeding  $M$  in two categories. The first category  $C_1{}$  consis of the primes  $q<M$  for which  $\nu_q(g(a_p))$  is unbounded, as  $p{}$  ranges over all the primes. The second category  $C_2{}$  consists of the remaining primes. 

Let  $C_1=\{q_1,\ldots,q_k\}$ . For each  $q_i\in C_1$  choose a prime number  $p_i$  for which  $\nu_{q_i}(g(a_{p_i}))>\log_{q_i}g(\lambda)$ . Lastly, choose a prime number  $p_0$  which is congruent to  $1$  modulo each  $p_i$  for  $1\leqslant i\leqslant k$ . Then,  $g(a_{p_0})\equiv g(\lambda)\bmod{g(a_{p_i})}$  for  $1\leqslant i\leqslant k$  so we cannot have  $\nu_{q_i}(g(a_{p_0}))>\log_{q_i}g(\lambda)$  by a size argument.

Thus,  $\nu_{q_i}(g(a_{p_0}))$  is bounded, for any  $q_i\in C_1$ . Furthermore,  $\nu_{q}(g(a_{p_0}))$  is bounded for every  $q\in C_2$  by definition. Therefore,  $\nu_{q}(g(a_{p_0}))$  is bounded for nay  $q<M$ . By our previous assumption, by taking  $p_0$  to be large enough, this means that  $g(a_{p_0})$  is bounded so, in particular,  $a_{p_0}$  is bounded for all large enough  $p_0\equiv 1\bmod{p_1\cdots p_k}$ .

We will prove that the entire sequence  $(a_i)_{i\geqslant 0}$  is bounded, which finishes the solution. Since  $\deg f\geqslant 2$  there exists some  $x_0$  such that, for all  $x{}$  with  $|x|>x_0$  we have  $|f(x)|>|x|.$  Then,  $|f(x)|>x_0$  so  $|f(f(x))|>|f(x)|$  and so on. Thus, if some  $|a_{i_0}|{}$  exceeds  $x_0$  then the sequence  $(|a_i|)_{i\geqslant i_0}$  is strictly increasing and it consits of integers, so it tends to infinity.

This evidently contradicts the fact that  $a_{p_0}$  is bounded for all large enough  $p_0\equiv 1\bmod{p_1\cdots p_k}$ . Therefore, there cannot be any  $a_i$  for which  $|a_i|>x_0$  so  $(a_i)_{i\geqslant 0}$  is bounded, as desired. *Note: by bounded, we refer to bounded below and above.***Remark.** The condition  $\deg f\geqslant 2$  is needed. Observe that the polynomial  $f(x)=2x+1$  yields the sequence  $a_i=2^i-1$  which evidently doesn't satisfy the desired condition.

stem_md:
In every cell of an  $n\times n$  board is written  $1$  or  $-1$ . At each step we may choose any of the  $4n-2$  diagonals of the board and change the signs of all the numbers on that diagonal. Determine the number of initial configurations from which, after a finite number of steps, we may arrive at a configuration where all products of numbers on rows and columns equal to  $1$ .

*Proposed by Pavel Ciurea*
solution_md:
Let  $r_1, r_2,\dots,r_n$  and  $c_1,c_2\dots,c_n$  be the product of the numbers on the  $i^\text{th}$  row/column.
We will prove that  $r_i\cdot r_{n+1-i}\cdot c_i\cdot c_{n+1-i}$ , where  $1\leq i\leq \frac{n}2$ , is constant, and (if  $n$  is odd),  $r_{\frac{n+1}2}\cdot c_{\frac{n+1}2}$  is constant as well:
Suppose  $1\leq i\leq \frac{n}2$ . Due to symmetry, we can suppose the diagonal that is changed is the one from  $(1,x)$  to  $(x,1)$ .
If  $x<i$ , none of the numbers  $r_i, r_{n+1-i}, c_i, c_{n+1-i}$  changes, so  $r_ir_{n+1-i}c_ic_{n+1-i}$  doesn't change.
If  $i\leq x<n+1-i$ ,  $r_i$  and  $c_i$  become  $-r_i$  and  $-c_i$ , so  $r_ir_{n+1-i}c_ic_{n+1-i}$  doesn't change.
If  $n+1-x\leq x$ , the numbers  $r_i, r_{n+1-i}, c_i, c_{n+1-i}$  all change, so  $r_ir_{n+1-i}c_ic_{n+1-i}$  doesn't change. 
If  $n$  is odd, notice that every diagonal intersects the  $\left(\frac{n+1}2\right)^\text{th}$  row if and only if in intersects the  $\left(\frac{n+1}2\right)^\text{th}$  column, so  $r_{\frac{n+1}2}c_{\frac{n+1}2}$  is constant as well.  $\blacksquare$ Since in the configuration where all products of numbers on rows and columns are equal to  $1$  all products  $r_ir_{n+1-i}c_ic_{n+1-i}$  are  $1$ , we conclude that if a configuration works, then  $r_ir_{n+1-i}c_ic_{n+1-i}=1$  for all  $1\leq i\leq n$  and (if  $n$  is odd)  $r_{\frac{n+1}2}\cdot c_{\frac{n+1}2}=1$ .
We will now prove that all such configurations can be brought to a configuration where all products of numbers on rows and columns are equal to  $1$ :
If  $n$  is even: We will use the following algorithm:
1) We make changes such that  $r_{\frac{n}2}=r_{\frac{n}2+1}=c_{\frac{n}2}=c_{\frac{n}2+1}=1$ ;
2) Prove that there exist moves such that we get  $r_{\frac{n}2-1}=r_{\frac{n}2+2}=c_{\frac{n}2-1}=c_{\frac{n}2+2}=1$  and don't change the  $r_{\frac{n}2}=r_{\frac{n}2+1}=c_{\frac{n}2}=c_{\frac{n}2+1}=1$ .
3) Repeat inductively.
Proof:
1) If  $r_{\frac{n}2}=r_{\frac{n}2+1}=c_{\frac{n}2}=c_{\frac{n}2+1}=1$ , we're done with this step.
If  $r_{\frac{n}2}=r_{\frac{n}2+1}=c_{\frac{n}2}=c_{\frac{n}2+1}=-1$ , we do 2 moves: on the  $\left(\frac{n}2,1\right)-\left(1,\frac{n}2\right)$  and  $\left(\frac{n}2+1,n\right)-\left(n,\frac{n}2+1\right)$  diagonals.
If  $r_{\frac{n}2}=r_{\frac{n}2+1}=1$  and  $c_{\frac{n}2}=c_{\frac{n}2+1}=-1$ , we do 2 moves: on the  $\left(\frac{n}2,1\right)-\left(1,\frac{n}2\right)$  and  $\left(\frac{n}2,n\right)-\left(1,\frac{n}2+1\right)$  diagonals.
If  $r_{\frac{n}2}=c_{\frac{n}2}=-1$  and  $r_{\frac{n}2+1}=c_{\frac{n}2+1}=1$ , we do a move on the  $\left(\frac{n}2,1\right)-\left(1,\frac{n}2\right)$  diagonal.
All other cases are similar versions of these last  $2$  cases.
2) Notice that applying the same kind of moves as in step 1) works, as none of those diagonals would cross the  $\left(\frac{n}2\right)^\text{th}$  and  $\left(\frac{n}2+1\right)^\text{th}$  lines and columns.
3) Now, inductively, we can actually consider all the lines and columns we've changed to have  $r_i=r_{n+1-i}=c_i=c_{n+1-i}=1$  to be all a single big "cross" and just repeat the whole algorithm.  $\blacksquare$ If  $n$  is odd, just do a move on  $\left(1,\frac{n+1}2\right)-\left(\frac{n+1}2,1\right)$  if  $r_{\frac{n+1}2}=c_{\frac{n+1}2}=1$ , and then just repeat the algorithm from the  $n$  - even case.
Now we just need to compute the number of such tables:
Let us complete the whole table at random, except the  $\left\lceil\frac{n}2\right\rceil-1$  cells  $(1,2),\dots,\left(1,\left\lceil\frac{n}2\right\rceil\right)$ .
Notice that, since we already know  $r_1,r_{\left\lceil\frac{n}2\right\rceil+1},r_{\left\lceil\frac{n}2\right\rceil+2},\dots,r_n$  and  $c_2,c_3,\dots,c_n$ , all the cells  $(1,x)$  will be uniquely filled from the  $r_x\cdot r_{n+1-x}\cdot c_x\cdot c_{n+1-x}=1$ , for all  $2\leq x\leq \left\lceil\frac{n}2\right\rceil$ .
Notice that now we just need to prove that  $r_1r_nc_1c_n=1$ , and we're done!
If  $n$  is even, by multiplying we get  $\prod_{1\leq i\leq \frac{n}2}(r_ir_{n+1-i}c_ic_{n+1-i})=\prod_{1\leq i,j\leq n}x_{i,j}^2=1$ , so  $r_1r_nc_1c_n=1$ .
If  $n$  is odd, by multiplying we get  $ (r_{\frac{n+1}2}\cdot c_{\frac{n+1}2})\prod_{1\leq i\leq \frac{n}2}(r_ir_{n+1-i}c_ic_{n+1-i})=\prod_{1\leq i,j\leq n}x_{i,j}^2=1$ , so  $r_1r_nc_1c_n=1$ .
Thus, since we randomly chose  $n^2+1-\left\lceil\frac{n}2\right\rceil$  cells, the number of configurations that work is  $2^{n^2+1-\left\lceil\frac{n}2\right\rceil}$ .

Find all positive integers  $n$  such that  $n+3$  divides  $3^{(n+1)!}-1$ .

*Proposed by Emanuel Mazăre*
solution_md:
The answer is  $\boxed{3 \nmid n , n \neq 2 }$ Notice that  $3^{(n+1)!}-1$  is not divisible by  $3$  so as  $n+3$ then,  $3^{\phi(n+3)} \equiv 1 \pmod{n+3}$ if  $n+3$  is composite thus,  $3^{(n+1)!}-1 \equiv 0 \pmod{n+3}$  (since  $\phi(n+3) \leq n+1$ )

if  $n+3$  is prime  $\geq 7$  thus,  $3^{n+2} \equiv 1 \pmod{n+3}$  
From  $n+2$  is composite greater than  $4$   $\implies$   $n+2 \mid (n+1)!$  done.

stem_md:
Consider a  $45\times 45$  table. We shall call *a snake* any succession of unit squares such that every square is either directly on top or directly to the right of the preceding square. Ana and Pavel play a game. With Ana starting first, they alternatively place the natural numbers from  $1$  to  $2025$  in the squares of the table, such that in the end every number appears exactly once. In the end, a snake will be called *a python* if the sum of squares of its numbers is divisible by  $25$ . Ana wins if the number of pythons is odd, and else, Pavel wins. Determine who has a winning strategy.

*Proposed by Emanuel Mazăre*
solution_md:
We claim that Ana wins. Label the rows  $1, ..., 45$  from bottom to top, the columns  $1, ..., 45$  from left to right,  $(i, j)$  be the square at row  $i$ , column  $j$ .

In addtion, we change the natural number  $a$  to  $a^2 \mod 25$ , for all  $a = 1, ..., 2025$ . So  $7$  becomes  $24$ ,  $10$  becomes  $0$ , ...
Then we have  $162$  copies of each of  $1, 4, 9, 16, 11, 24, 14, 6, 21, 19$ , and  $405$  copies of  $0$ .

First, Ana place a  $0$  at square  $(1, 1)$ . Then, Ana perform the following algorithm:
+ If Pavel place a number  $n$  at square  $(i, j)$  where  $j \neq i$ , Then Ana place the number  $n$  at square  $(j, i)$  (i.e. the number opposite to it across the bottom left-top right diagonal)
+ If Pavel place a number  $n$  at some square on said diagonal, Ana place a number  $n$  at some other square on the diagonal. The position does not matter.

Then the entire board is symmetric across the main diagonal (or the line  $y = x$ ). So all pythons that has at least one square not on the main diagonal can be grouped into pairs, such that the snakes in each pair is each other's reflection across the main diagonal. Finally, there are an odd number of  $0$  on the main diagonal, so the total number of pythons is odd.

stem_md:
Let  $n$  be a positive integer and  $\{p_1,p_2,\dots ,p_n\}$  a set of distrinct prime numbers. Let  $N=p_1p_2\dots p_n$ . Prove that there exist at most  $3^n$  pairs  $(a,b)$  of positive divisors of  $N$  with the property that  $a+b$  is a perfect square.

*Proposed by Andrei Chiriță*
solution_md: We will prove the following claim: Claim 1: Let $d_1,d_2$ be two positive coprime divisors of $N$ . Then the set $A_{(d_1,d_2)}=\{(e_1,e_2)\mid e_1\mid N, e_2\mid N, e_1=d_1m, e_2=d_2m, m\in\mathbb{N}\}$ contains at most one pair of divisors $(a,b)\in A_{(d_1,d_2)}$ such that $a+b$ is a perfect square. Proof: Suppose there existed two distinct pairs in $A_{(d_1,d_2)}$ with the given property. This means there exist $m_1\neq m_2$ , $m_id_j\mid N$ for all $i,j\in\{1,2\}$ , $m_1,m_2\in\mathbb{N}$ , such that $m_1(d_1+d_2)$ and $m_2(d_1+d_2)$ are perfect squares. So $m_1\mid N$ , $m_2\mid N$ , thus implying that $\nu_p(m_i)\leq 1,\forall i\in\{1,2\}$ . Since $m_1\neq m_2\implies$ there exists a prime $p$ that divides one of the numbers and doesn't divide the other. WLOG suppose $p$ divides $m_1$ and doesn't divide $m_2\implies \nu_p(m_1)=1$ and $\nu_p(m_2)=0$ . $m_1(d_1+d_2)$ and $m_2(d_1+d_2)$ are perfect squares $\implies \nu_p(m_1)+\nu_p(d_1+d_2)\equiv\nu_p(m_2)+\nu_p(d_1+d_2)\equiv0\pmod 2$ , contradiction. $\blacksquare$ Thus we can conclude that the number of pairs of divisors $(a,b)$ of $N$ such that $a+b$ is a perfect square is at most equal to the number of pairs of comprime positive divisors of $N$ . Let $(d_1,d_2)$ be such a pair. Notice that for all primes $p_i$ there are three possible cases: either $p_i\mid d_1$ , either $p_i\mid d_2$ , either $p_i$ doesn't divide any of the two. Thus there are $3^n$ such possible pairs.

Let  $ABCD$  be a quadrilateral with non-parallel opposite sides. Lines  $AB$  and  $CD$  intersect at  $X$ , while  $(ACX)$  and  $(BDX)$  meet a second time at  $Y$ . If  $U$  and  $V$  are the  $Y$ -Humpty points of  $\triangle YAB$  and  $\triangle YCD$ , prove that lines  $AD$ ,  $BC$  and  $UV$  intersect at  a common point.

*Proposed by Emanuel Mazăre*
solution_md: Invert around $Y$ .**New Problem Statement:** $ABCD$ is a quadrilateral where $AC\cap BD=X$ and $(ABX)\cap (CDX)=Y$ . Let $U,V$ be the intersection of tangents to $(ABX)$ at $A,B$ and $(CDX)$ at $C,D$ respectively. Prove that $(YAD),(YBC),(YUV)$ concur. Let $UB,VC$ meet $(YBC)$ at $P,R$ and $UA,VD$ meet $(YAD)$ at $Q,S$ . We have $\measuredangle CPB=180-\measuredangle BYC=180-\measuredangle PBD-\measuredangle BDC $ which implies $P\in CD$ . Similarily $Q\in CD$ and $R,S\in AB$ . Note that $\measuredangle QPU=\measuredangle VRS$ and $\measuredangle UQP=\measuredangle RSV$ thus, $UPQ\sim VRS$ . \[\frac{Pow(U,(YBC))}{Pow(U,(YAD))}=\frac{UB.UP}{UA.UQ}=\frac{UP}{UQ}=\frac{VR}{VS}=\frac{VC.VR}{VD.VS}=\frac{Pow(V,(YBC))}{Pow(V,(YAD))}\] Coaxiality lemma finishes by the equality as desired. $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $ S $  be the first quadrant and  $ T:S\longrightarrow S $  be a transformation that takes the reciprocal of the coordinates of the points that belong to its domain. Define an *S-line* to be the intersection of a line with  $ S. $ **a)** Show that the fixed points of  $ T $  lie on any fixed S-line of  $ T. $ **b)** Find all fixed S-lines of  $ T. $ *Gabriel Popa*
solution_md:
I see. Thanks for the clarification.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Clearly, a null-set is a fixed S-line of  $T$ .

Now, consider a nonempty S-line. Let  $y=ax+b$  be the equation of this S-line. For any point  $(x,ax+b)$  on this line, then the point  $\left(\frac1x,\frac1{ax+b}\right)$  must also lie on this line.

The equation  $$ \frac1{ax+b}=\frac ax+b $$  must be true for all  $x$ .  $$ \frac1{ax+b}=\frac ax+b\implies x=a(ax+b)+bx(ax+b)\implies abx^2+(a^2-1)x+ab+b^2=0 $$  This gives us  $$ \begin{cases}ab=0
a^2-1=0
ab+b^2=0\end{cases} $$  Solving this gives us two solutions:  $(a,b)=(1,0),(-1,0)$ .

Therefore, the only possible S-lines are  $y=x$  and  $y=-x$ . However, the line  $y=-x$  lies entirely outside  $S$ , so this wouldn't be considered.

Hence, the only fixed S-lines of  $T$  are  $\boxed{\varnothing}$ , and  $\boxed{\{(x,y)\mid x=y\land x,y>0\}}$ .</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Romania Contests/Other Romanian Contests/Romania - Local Contests/Alexandru Myller/2003 Alexandru Myller/1928021.json

stem_md: Let be a natural number  $ n, $  a positive real number  $ \lambda , $  and a complex number  $ z. $  Prove the following inequalities.  $$  0\le -\lambda +\frac{1}{n}\sum_{\stackrel{w\in\mathbb{C}}{w^n=1 }} \left| z-\lambda w \right|\le |z|  $$  *Gheorghe Iurea*
solution_md:
I don't see why the version cited in #4 should be wrong, in my eyes it seems to be trivially equivalent to the modified version currently stated in #1.
Certainly it is true for  $z=0$  since it just says  $0 \le 0 \le 0$ .
In any case, to prove the general case we can substitute  $z=\lambda z'$  if necessary so that we may w.l.o.g. assume that  $\lambda=1$  i.e. we need to prove that
\[1 \le \frac{\sum_{\zeta} \vert z-\zeta\vert}{n} \le 1+\vert z\vert\]
where the sum runs over all  $n$ -th roots of unity  $\zeta$ . Here, the upper bound is trivial from the triangle inequality since  $\vert z-\zeta\vert \le \vert z\vert+1$ . In fact, an application of AM-QM shows that the (better) upper bound  $\sqrt{\vert z\vert^2+1}$  is admissible.
For the lower bound: If  $n$  is even, we can just pair the values  $\zeta$  and  $-\zeta$  and note that
\[\vert z-\zeta\vert+\vert z+\zeta\vert \ge 2\vert \zeta\vert=2\]
by the triangle inequality which gives the desired estimate. By a similar argument, for odd  $n$ , it suffices to prove it in the case where  $n$  is prime. However, this does not seem to simplify the problem significantly...

stem_md: Prove that  $$  (n+2)^n=\prod_{k=1}^{n+1} \sum_{l=1}^{n+1} le^{\frac{2i\pi k (n-l+1)}{n+2}} ,  $$  for any natural number  $ n. $ *Mihai Piticari*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let the sum be  $S_k$ .  $$ S_k=\sum_{l=1}^{n+1}le^{\frac{2i\pi k(n-l+1)}{n+2}} $$  Multiplying both sides by  $e^{\frac{2i\pi k}{n+2}}$ ,  $$ e^{\frac{2i\pi k}{n+2}}S_k=\sum_{l=1}^{n+1} le^{\frac{2i\pi k(n-l+2)}{n+2}} $$    $$ e^{\frac{2i\pi k}{n+2}}S_k=\sum_{l=0}^n(l+1)e^{\frac{2i\pi k(n-l+1)}{n+2}} $$  Subtracting the two,  $$ \left(e^{\frac{2i\pi k}{n+2}}-1\right)S_k=\sum_{l=0}^ne^{\frac{2i\pi k(n-l+1)}{n+2}}-(n+1) $$  Now, we simplify this.  $$ \left(e^{\frac{2i\pi k}{n+2}}-1\right)S_k=e^{\frac{2i\pi k(n+1)}{n+2}}\left(\frac{1-e^{-\frac{2i\pi k(n+1)}{n+2}}}{1-e^{-\frac{2i\pi k}{n+2}}}\right)-(n+1) $$    $$ \left(e^{\frac{2i\pi k}{n+2}}-1\right)S_k=\frac{e^{\frac{2i\pi k(n+1)}{n+2}}-1}{1-e^{-\frac{2i\pi k}{n+2}}}-(n+1) $$    $$ \left(e^{\frac{2i\pi k}{n+2}}-1\right)S_k=\frac{e^{\frac{i\pi k(2n+3)}{n+2}}-e^{\frac{i\pi k}{n+2}}}{e^{\frac{i\pi k}{n+2}}-e^{-\frac{i\pi k}{n+2}}}-(n+1) $$    $$ \left(e^{\frac{2i\pi k}{n+2}}-1\right)S_k=\frac{e^{-\frac{i\pi k}{n+2}}-e^{\frac{i\pi k}{n+2}}}{e^{\frac{i\pi k}{n+2}}-e^{-\frac{i\pi k}{n+2}}}-(n+1) $$    $$ \left(e^{\frac{2i\pi k}{n+2}}-1\right)S_k=-1-(n+1) $$    $$ \left(e^{\frac{2i\pi k}{n+2}}-1\right)S_k=-(n+2) $$  Dividing both sides by  $\left(e^{\frac{2i\pi k}{n+2}}-1\right)$ .  $$ S_k=\frac{-(n+2)}{e^{\frac{2i\pi k}{n+2}}-1} $$    $$ S_k=\frac{-(n+2)e^{\frac{-i\pi k}{n+2}}}{e^{\frac{i\pi k}{n+2}}-e^{\frac{-i\pi k}{n+2}}} $$    $$ S_k=\frac{-(n+2)e^{\frac{-i\pi k}{n+2}}}{2i\sin\frac{\pi k}{n+2}} $$  Now, taking the product of  $S_k$ \begin{align*}
\prod_{k=1}^{n+1}S_k&=\prod_{k=1}^{n+1}\frac{-(n+2)e^{\frac{-i\pi k}{n+2}}}{2i\sin\frac{\pi k}{n+2}}
&=\frac{(-(n+2))^{n+1}e^{\frac{-i\pi\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}2}{n+2}}}{(2i)^{n+1}\sin\frac{\pi}{n+2}\sin\frac{2\pi}{n+2}\cdots\sin\frac{(n+1)\pi}{n+2}}
&=\frac{(-(n+2))^{n+1}(-i)^{n+1}}{(2i)^{n+1}\sin\frac{\pi}{n+2}\sin\frac{2\pi}{n+2}\cdots\sin\frac{(n+1)\pi}{n+2}}
&=\frac{(n+2)^{n+1}}{2^{n+1}\sin\frac{\pi}{n+2}\sin\frac{2\pi}{n+2}\cdots\sin\frac{(n+1)\pi}{n+2}}
\end{align*}
And according to [this link,](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/8385/prove-that-prod-k-1n-1-sin-frack-pin-fracn2n-1), we have  $$ \sin\frac{\pi}{n+2}\sin\frac{2\pi}{n+2}\cdots\sin\frac{(n+1)\pi}{n+2}=\frac{n+2}{2^{n+1}} $$  Therefore,
\begin{align*}
\prod_{k=1}^{n+1}S_k&=\frac{(n+2)^{n+1}}{2^{n+1}\sin\frac{\pi}{n+2}\sin\frac{2\pi}{n+2}\cdots\sin\frac{(n+1)\pi}{n+2}}
&=\frac{(n+2)^{n+1}}{2^{n+1}\cdot\frac{n+2}{2^{n+1}}}
&=(n+2)^n\end{align*}
which is what we wanted to prove.</details>

stem_md:
Let be a nonnegative integer  $ n. $  Prove that there exists an increasing and finite sequence of positive real numbers,  $ 
\left( a_k \right)_{0\le k\le n} , $  that satisfy the equality  $$  a_0/0! +a_1/1! +a_2/2! +\cdots +a_n/n! =1/n! ,  $$  and the inequality  $$  a_0+a_1+a_2+\cdots +a_n<\frac{3}{2^n} .  $$  *Dorin Andrica*
solution_md:
It's a weird condition.
By choosing the  $a_i$  all equal to  $\frac{1}{n!\left(\frac{1}{0!}+\frac{1}{1!}+\dots+\frac{1}{n!}\right)}$  (or arbitrarily close to that if you require strictly increasing) it suffices to show that
\[\frac{n+1}{n!\left(\frac{1}{0!}+\frac{1}{1!}+\dots+\frac{1}{n!}\right)}<\frac{3}{2^n}\]
This is clear for  $n=0, n=1$  so that it suffices to prove that
\[\frac{1}{(n-1)!}<\frac{3}{2^n}\]
for  $n \ge 2$ . Which is easily seen by induction.

stem_md: Calculate  $ \int_0^{2\pi }\prod_{i=1}^{2002} cos^i (it) dt. $ *Dorin Andrica*
solution_md:
Here is my approach. Since  $ I = \int_0^{2\pi }\prod_{i=1}^{2002} cos^i (it) dt = \int_0^{\pi }\prod_{i=1}^{2002} cos^i (it) dt +  \int_{\pi}^{2\pi }\prod_{i=1}^{2002} cos^i (it) dt= I_1 + I_2$ .
 So we will calculate one by one. We have a lemma:
Let  $g(x)$  be continuous and  $a,b \in \mathbb{R}$  so:  $\int _{a}^{b} g(x)dx = \int _{a}^{b} g(a+b - x)dx$ And since two integral can be similarly calculate so we will just do the first one:   $$   I_1 =  \int_0^{\pi } \prod_{i=1}^{1001} cos^{2i} (2it) \prod_{i=0}^{1000} cos^{2i+1} ((2i+1)t) dt  $$  Then applying the lemma gives us:  $$ I_1 = \int_0^{\pi } \prod_{i=1}^{1001} cos^{2i} (2i(\pi - t)) \prod_{i=0}^{1000} cos^{2i+1} ((2i+1)(\pi - t) ) dt  $$  Using cosine properties give us:   $$ I_1 = \int_0^{\pi } \prod_{i=1}^{1001} cos^{2i} (2it) (-1)^{1001} \prod_{i=0}^{1000} cos^{2i+1} ((2i+1)t) dt = - I_1 $$   
Or we have  $I_1 = 0$ . Using similar transformation also gives us  $I_2=0$ . Then  $I=0$

stem_md: **a)** Prove that the function  $ 1\le t\mapsto\int_{1}^t\frac{\sin x}{x^n} dx $  has an horizontal asymptote, for any natural number  $ n. $ **b)** Calculate  $ \lim_{n\to\infty }\lim_{t\to\infty }\int_{1}^t\frac{\sin x}{x^n} . $ *Mihai Piticari*
solution_md:
a) We need the convergence of  $\int_1^\infty {{\sin x dx}\over {x^n}}$ . For  $n\ge 2$  we have absolute convergence since  $|\sin x|\le 1$  and for  $n=1$  we can use the Dirichlet test.
b) We need  $\lim_n  \int_1^\infty {{\sin x dx}\over {x^n}}$  which is obviously 0 since for  $n\ge 2$  we have  $|\int_1^\infty {{\sin x dx}\over {x^n}}|\le \int_1^\infty {{dx}\over {x^n}}={1\over {n-1}}$ .

solution_md:
Wrinig formula of surface, we only need to prove
\[ |\sin(AOB)\sin(COD)-\sin(BOC)\sin(DOA)|=\sin(AOC)\sin(BOD) \]
But just take a circle with center  $O$  and let  $A',B',C',D'$  be the intersections of this circle with  $OA,OB,OC,OD$ .
Now the above equality (in sines) becomes the ptolemy's theorem for the cyclic  $A'B'C'D'$ .

stem_md: Find the real numbers  $ x>1 $  having the property that  $ \sqrt[n]{\lfloor x^n \rfloor } $  is an integer for any natural number  $ n\ge 2. $ *Mihai Piticari* and *Dan Popescu*
solution_md: This is equivalent to finding all numbers x for which for all n>=2, there exists an integer a such that:  $$ a^n \le x^n < a^n+1 $$  this implies  $$ a \le x < (a^n+1)^{\frac{1}{n}} $$  Clearly a must be fixed as  $a = floor(x)$  because  $(a^n+1)^{\frac{1}{n}}  < (a+1) \iff a^n+1 < (a+1)^n$ Also  $\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} (a^n+1)^{\frac{1}{n}} = a$  from above, and so we see that the fractional part must be zero implying that x is an integer. And all integers >=2 work, so this is the answer.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Romania Contests/Other Romanian Contests/Romania - Local Contests/Alexandru Myller/2004 Alexandru Myller/2173456.json

stem_md:
Let be a natural number  $ a\ge 2. $ **a)** Show that there is no infinite sequence  $ \left( k_n \right)_{n\ge 1} $  of pairwise distinct natural numbers greater than  $ 1 $  having the property that the sequence  $ \left( a^{1/k_n} \right)_{n\ge 1} $  is a geometric progression.**b)** Show that there are finite sequences  $ \left( l_i \right)_i, $  of any length, of pairwise distinct natural numbers greater than  $ 1 $  with the property that  $ \left( a^{1/l_i} \right)_{i} $  is a geometric progression.


*Bogdan Enescu*
solution_md:
a) By assumption the sequence  $\left( a^{1/k_n} \right)_n$  is not constant, hence it is either strictly increasing or strictly decreasing. The former is impossible, since then  $(k_n)_n$  would be strictly decreasing, which contradicts the fact that each  $k_n$  is an integer greater than  $1$ .
Thus the sequence  $\left( a^{1/k_n} \right)_n$  is strictly decreasing, which means that its common ratio is less than  $1$ . But this implies that  $\lim_{n \to \infty}  a^{1/k_n} = 0$ . On the other hand,  $ a^{1/k_n} >a^0=1$  for each  $n$ , which is a contradiction.
b) Let  $N$  be an integer greater than  $1$ . Choose  $k_n = \frac{N!}{n}$  for  $n=1,2, \ldots, N$ .  Then the sequence  $(1/k_n)$  is an arithmetic progression, since  $\frac{1}{k_n}=\frac{n}{N!}$ . Thus  $\left( a^{1/k_n} \right)_n$  is a geometric progression of length  $N$ .

**a)** Let  $ \left( x_n \right)_{n\ge 1} $  be a sequence of real numbers having the property that  $ \left| x_{n+1} -x_n \right|\leqslant 1/2^n, $  for any  $ n\geqslant 1. $ Show that  $ \left( x_n \right)_{n\ge 1} $  is convergent.**b)** Create a sequence  $ \left( y_n \right)_{n\ge 1} $  of real numbers that has the following properties: $ \text{(i) } \lim_{n\to\infty } \left( y_{n+1} -y_n \right) = 0 $  $ \text{(ii) } $  is bounded $ \text{(iii) } $  is divergent


*Eugen Popa*
solution_md:
**a)** Let $ \left( x_n \right)_{n\ge 1} $ be a sequence of real numbers having the property that $ \left| x_{n+1} -x_n \right|\leqslant 1/2^n, $ for any $ n\geqslant 1. $ Show that $ \left( x_n \right)_{n\ge 1} $ is convergent.
You can show that $(x_n)_{n\geq 1}$ is a Cauchy sequence. Here is the main calculation: $$ |x_{n} - x_{m}| \leq \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} |x_{k+1} - x_k| \leq \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} 2^{-k} \le 2^{-(m-1)}. $$ Now we choose $m$ large enough such that $2^{-(m-1)}<\varepsilon.$
**b)** Create a sequence $ \left( y_n \right)_{n\ge 1} $ of real numbers that has the following properties: $ \text{(i) } \lim_{n\to\infty } \left( y_{n+1} -y_n \right) = 0 $ $ \text{(ii) } $ is bounded $ \text{(iii) } $ is divergent
I think $y_n = \sin(\sqrt{n})$ works. The conditions (ii) and (iii) are easy to check. For (i), use the following: $$ |\sin(\sqrt{n+1})- \sin(\sqrt{n})|\leq |\sqrt{n+1}- \sqrt{n}| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n+1}+\sqrt{n}}\to 0. $$

stem_md: On a non-rhombus parallelogram  $ ABCD, $  the vertex  $ B $  is projected on  $ AC $  in the point  $ E. $  The perpendicular on  $ BD $  thru  $ E $  intersects the lines  $ BC $  and  $ AB $  in  $ F $  and  $ G, $  respectively. Show that  $ EF=EG $  if and only if  $ \angle ABC=90^{\circ } . $ *Mircea Becheanu*
solution_md:
***My solution.***
Let  $H$  be line  $EF$  intersection point with  $BD$ .

If  $\angle ABC=90^{\circ}$ , then parallelogram  $ABCD$  becomes a rectangle. 
So  $\angle ABD=\angle ACD=\angle CBE$  (by similar triangles).
Since  $\angle BHF=\angle GBF =90^{\circ}$  and  $\angle BFH=\angle GFB$ , then  $\triangle GBF\sim \triangle BHF$ , so  $\angle HBF=\angle BGF$ , which implies  $\angle EGB=\angle EBG$ , which furthermore implies that  $\angle EBF=\angle EFB$ , thus  $EG=EB=EF$ .

If  $EF=EG$ , then extend diagram such that  $EB=EK$  and  $B$ ,  $E$  and  $K$  lie on the same line. Now we know that  $BFKG$  is a parallelogram, so parallelogram  $BFKG$  is similar to parallelogram  $BCDA$ . We also see that  $E$  and  $H$  are defined similarly with respect to a parallelogram  $BCDA$  and  $BFKG$ , respectively, so  $\triangle GFB\sim \triangle CAB$ . So we easily get that  $DK\parallel AC$  and  $AK=AB=CD$ , so  $ACKD$  is an isosceles trapezium and by symmetry, we get  $A$ ,  $B$ ,  $C$ ,  $K$  and  $D$ . This is good because now we get by angle chasing that  $EGB$  is an isosceles triangle and thus  $EG=EB=EF$  and we conclude that  $\angle ABC=90^{\circ}$ .

stem_md: Show that the equation  $ (x+y)^{-1}=x^{-1}+y^{-1} $  has a solution in the field of integers modulo  $ p $  if and only if  $ p $  is a prime congruent to  $ 1 $  modulo  $ 3. $ *Mihai Piticari*
solution_md:
Rewriting  $(x+y)({1\over x}+{1\over y})=1$  gives  $x^2+xy+y^2=1$ . First suppose that there is a solution. If  $p=2$  we have  $x=y=1$ ,  contradiction.. Otherwise we write  $(2x+y)^2+3y^2=0$ . If  $p=3$  then  $x=y \implies 3x^2=1$ , contradiction. For  $p
ot=2,3$  we note that  $-3$  is a  square modulo  $p$  (since  $y
ot=0$ ) and we can use quadratic reciprocity.
We have  $({{-1}\over p})=(-1)^{{{p-1}\over 2}},({3\over p})=(-1)^{{{p-1}\over 2}}({p\over 3})$  hence  $p\equiv 1(3)$ .
If  $p\equiv 1(3)$  then  $t^2\equiv -3(p)$  has a solution. Now take  $2x=t-1,y=1$ , which works since  $t
ot=1$ .

stem_md: $\lim_{n\to\infty } \sum_{1\le i\le j\le n} \frac{\ln (1+i/n)\cdot\ln (1+j/n)}{\sqrt{n^4+i^2+j^2}}  $ *Gabriel Mîrșanu* and *Andrei Nedelcu*
solution_md:
With  $a:=\sqrt{n^4+i^2+j^2}$  we have  $|{1\over {n^2}}-{1\over a}|={{a-n^2}\over {an^2}}={{a^2-n^4}\over {an^2(a+n^2)}}={{i^2+j^2}\over {an^2(a+n^2)}}\le {{2n^2}\over {an^2(a+n^2)}}\le {1\over {n^4}}$ .
Hence we may consider the equivalent limit  $\lim {1\over {n^2}}\sum_{1\le i\le j\le n} \ln (1+{i\over n})\ln (1+{j\over n})$ . 
This is the limit of a 2-dimensional Riemann sum and equals  $\int_A \ln (1+x)\ln(1+y) dx dy$  where  $A$  is the triangle  $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1)$ .
By symmetry this is  ${1\over 2} \int_{[0,1]^2} \ln(1+x)\ln(1+y) dx dy={1\over 2}(\int_0^1 \ln (1+x) dx)^2={{(2\ln 2-1)^2}\over 2}$ .

stem_md: Prove that the number of nilpotent elements of a commutative ring with an order greater than  $ 8 $  and congruent to  $ 3 $  modulo  $ 6 $  is at most a third of the order of the ring.
solution_md:
Let  $N(R)$  be the set (ideal, in fact) of the nilpotent elements of a ring  $R.$  

Firstly, the claim in your problem is not necessarily true for rings that don't have  $1,$  the multiplicative identity. For example, for any positive integer  $n,$  consider the commutative ring   $$ R:=\left \{\begin{pmatrix}0 & x  0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}: \ \ \ x \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\right \}. $$  Then  $R^2=(0)$  and so  $N(R)=R.$ Secondly, the claim in your problem is almost trivially true for rings that have  $1$  and we don't need that condition on the order of the ring; what we need is for the ring to have odd order (thus  $ \ge 3$ ). Well,  $N(R)$  is a subgroup of  $(R,+)$  and hence  $|R|=k|N(R)|$  for some integer  $k \ge 1.$  We can't have  $k=1$  because then  $R=N(R)$  but  $1 \in R \setminus N(R).$  Also we can't have  $k=2$  because  $|R|$  is odd. So  $k \ge 3$  and thus  $|N(R)| \le \frac{1}{3}|R|.$

stem_md: For any natural number  $ m, \quad\lim_{n\to\infty } n^{1+m} \int_{0}^1 e^{-nx}\ln \left( 1+x^m \right) dx =m! .  $ *Gheorghe Iurea*
solution_md:
The general idea is to do integration by parts  $m+1$  times. 

Let   $$ f(x):=\ln(1+x^m)=x^m-\frac{x^{2m}}{2} + \cdots, \ \ \ \ \ \ \ I_n:= n^{1+m} \int_{0}^1 e^{-nx}\ln \left( 1+x^m \right) dx. $$  It's clear that   $$ f^{(k)}(0)=0, \ \ \ \ 0 \le k \le m-1, \ \ \ \ \ \ \ f^{(m)}(0)=m!. $$  Now do integration parts  $f(x)=u, \ \ e^{-nx}dx=dv$  to get   $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}I_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}n^m\int_0^1 e^{-nx}f'(x) \ dx. $$  Do integration by parts again with  $f'(x)=u, \ \ e^{-nx}dx=dv$  to get  $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}I_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{m-1}\int_0^1e^{-nx}f''(x) \ dx $$  and keep doing integration by parts  $m+1$  times to eventually get  $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}I_n=m!+\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^1e^{-nx}f^{(m+1)}(x) \ dx. $$  The result now follows because  $f^{(m+1)}(x)$  is continuous on  $[0,1]$  and so it is bounded, hence   $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^1e^{-nx}f^{(m+1)}(x) \ dx=0 $$  because  $\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^1e^{-nx} \ dx=0.$
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Romania Contests/Other Romanian Contests/Romania - Local Contests/Alexandru Myller/2004 Alexandru Myller/2175355.json

candidates: An different approach: Let  $I_m (n) = n^{1+m} \int_{0}^1 e^{-nx}\ln \left( 1+x^m \right) dx =m!$  which means we need to prove that  $ \lim_{n\to\infty } I_m (n) = m!$ . Integrating by parts gives us:  $$  n^{1+m}\cdot\int_{0}^{1} e^{-nx}\ln \left( 1+x^m \right) dx  = -~n^{m}e^{-nx}\ln\left(1+x^m\right)\Big|_0^1 + m\cdot n^m\int_{0}^{1} \frac{x^{m-1}\cdot e^{-nx}}{1+x^m} dx $$  As  $n \to \infty$ , it is clear that  $n^{m}e^{-n}\ln\left(2\right) \to 0$ . Hence:  $$ I_m(n) = m\cdot n^m\int_{0}^{1} \frac{x^{m-1}\cdot e^{-nx}}{1+x^m} dx, n \to \infty $$  Now we have to inequality which we can apply Squeeze theorem:  $$ n^m\int_{0}^{1} \frac{x^{m-1}\cdot e^{-nx}}{1+x^m} dx, n \to \infty \leq n^m\int_{0}^{1} x^{m-1}\cdot e^{-nx} dx = \int_{0}^{n} t^{m-1} e^{-t} ~dt, t = nx $$  And:  $$  n^m\int_{0}^{1} \frac{x^{m-1}\cdot e^{-nx}}{1+x^m} dx \geq n^m\int_{0}^{1} \frac{x^{m-1}\cdot e^{-nx}}{1+x} dx = \int_{0}^{n} \frac{t^{m-1} e^{-t}}{1+\frac{t}{n}}~dt = \int_{0}^{n} t^{m-1} e^{-t}~dt ~-~ \int_{0}^{n} \frac{t^{m} e^{-t}}{n+t}~dt  $$    $$ \geq\int_{0}^{n} t^{m-1} e^{-t}~dt~-~\int_{0}^{n} \frac{t^{m} e^{-t}}{n}~dt $$  As the result:  $$ m!=m\cdot \lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{0}^{n} t^{m-1} e^{-t}~dt~-~\int_{0}^{n} \frac{t^{m} e^{-t}}{n}~dt \leq\lim_{n\to\infty} I_m(n)\leq m\cdot\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{0}^{n} t^{m-1}e^{-t}~dt =m! $$  By Squeeze theorem,  $\lim_{n\to \infty} I_m (n) = m!$ . We are done

By using  $\ln(1+x)=x+O(x^2)$ we have by using  $u=nx$ : $n^{1+m} \int_0^1 e^{-nx}\ln(1+x^m)dx=\int_0^n e^{-u}n^m\ln(1+(\frac un)^m/2)du=\int_0^n u^me^{-u}du+\int_0^n e^{-u}O(\frac{u^{2m}}{n^m})dx$  $=\int_0^nu^me^{-u}du+O(n^{-m})$  since  $\int_0^n x^{2m}e^{-x}dx<\infty$  
Therefore the limit is m!

solution_md:
Let $ x,y,z $ be numbers distinct from $ -1 $ that verify the equation $$ \frac{1}{1+a} +\frac{1}{1+b} +\frac{1}{1+c} =\frac{3}{2} . $$ Prove that if $ abc=1, $ then $ a $ or $ b $ or $ c $ is equal to $ 1. $
Both equalities leads to $a+b+c=ab+bc+ca$ . Therefore: $$ (a-1)(b-1)(c-1)=abc+a+b+c-ab-bc-ca-1=0 $$ Therefore, one of the numbers is equal to $1$ .

stem_md:
Let  $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$  be a continous function with the property that there exists a constant  $\lambda\in\mathbb R$  so that for every  $x\in[a,b]$  there exists a  $y\in[a,b]-\{x\}$  s.t.  $\int_x^yf(x)dx=\lambda$ . Prove that the function  $f$  has at least two zeros in  $(a,b)$ .
*Eugen Paltanea*
solution_md:
Assume first that  $f$  has no  $0$ 's in  $(a,b)$ . We may assume WLOG that  $f>0$  on  $(a,b)$ . If  $\lambda<0$ , we can see that it's  $\ge 0$  by pushing  $x$  as close to  $a$  as we want. On the other hand, if it's  $>0$ , we can see that it's  $\le 0$ , by pushing  $x$  as close to  $b$  as we want. We have thus got a contradiction, so  $f$  has at least a root  $x_0$  in  $(a,b)$ .

Assume now that  $f>0$  on  $(x_0,b)$  and  $f<0$  on  $(a,x_0)$ . Then  $\lambda>0$ , since we can take  $x=x_0$ . Again, we push  $x$  arbitrarily close to  $a$  and  $b$  to find  $\int^b_{x_0}f(t)dt\ge\int^a_{x_0}f(t)dt$  and  $\int^b_{x_0}f(t)dt\le\int^a_{x_0}f(t)dt$  respectively. This means that  $\int^b_{x_0}f(t)dt=\int^a_{x_0}f(t)dt$ . Making once more  $x\to a$ ,  $\sup_{y\in[a,b]}\lambda^y_x f(t)dt$  can be made smaller than any positive real, and, in particular, smaller than  $\lambda$ , which is a contradiction.

Sorry I didn't post the details of those claims, but they look pretty intuitive :).

stem_md:
Let  $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$  be an increasing function. Prove that if  $\int_0^1f(x)dx=\int_0^1\left(\int_0^xf(t)dt\right)dx=0$  then  $f(x)=0,\forall x\in(0,1)$ .

*Mihai Piticari*
solution_md:
$F(x)=\int^x_0 f(t)dt$  is a continuous function which is also convex. This is because it's continuous and semiconvex, i.e.  $F(\frac {x+y}2)\le\frac{F(x)+F(y)}2$ . To show the semiconvexity, translate it to  $\int^{\frac {x+y}2}_0 f(t)dt\le\frac{\int^x_0 f(t)dt+\int^y_0 f(t)dt}2$ . Assuming  $x\le y$ , what we have to show is  $2\int^{\frac{x+y}2}_x f(t)dt\le\int^y_x f(t)dt$ , which follows immediately from the fact that  $f$  is increasing.

Now, since a convex function on an interval reaches its maximum in one of the interval's ends, and our function  $F$  is  $0$  in both ends, it means that it's  $\le 0$ . Since its integral over  $[0,1]$  is also  $0$ , we get  $F\equiv 0$ , and from here the fact that  $f$  is identically null on  $(0,1)$  follows.

stem_md:
Let  $K$  be a finite field and  $f:K\to K^*$ . Prove that there is a reducible polynomial  $P\in K[X]$  s.t.  $P(x)=f(x),\forall x\in K$ .

solution_md:
Indeed the condition K* was superfluous, just as the condition P reducible was uninteresting: just construct any polynomial  $P_1$  with  $P_1\equiv f$  and then consider  $P=P_1\cdot Q^2$ , where  $Q$  takes only the value 1. And voila,  $P$  will be reducible.

  I found it interesting that during the contest the students gave many different constructions of  $Q$ : i remember now only  $Q=x^n-x+1$ , where  $|K|=n$ , and  $Q=-2\cdot x^{n-1}+1$  (which gives 1 or -1, which is ok) and  $Q=\prod_{a\in K}(x-a)+1$ ... and others

 Also there were a few other ways to construct P : one way is by Lagrange, as you said , or inductively:

 Say  $P_i$  "satisfies" a maximal set  $A_i=\{x\in K| P_i(x)=f(x)\}$ . Then choose  $P_{i+1}(x)=P_i(x)\cdot(1+L\prod_{a\in A_i}(x-a))$ , where  $L\in K$  is chosen such that  $P_{i+1}$  satisfies another  $b\in K\setminus A_i$ . But  $P_{i+1}$  obviously satisfies all  $b\in A_{i}$  ... and so on...

stem_md: For an odd prime  $ p, $  show that  $ \sum_{k=1}^{p-1} \frac{k^p-k}{p}\equiv \frac{1+p}{2}\pmod p . $
solution_md:
**Lemma:** For every odd prime  $p$  and integer  $a$ , we have  $p^2|a^p+(p-a)^p$ .**Proof:**  $(p-a)^p+a^p\equiv \dbinom{p}{1}pa^{p-1}-\dbinom{p}{0}a^p+a^p\equiv 0-a^p+a^p\equiv 0\pmod{p^2}$ .

Hence,   $$ \sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac{k^p-k}p=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} k^p}p-\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} k}p=\frac{(1^p+(p-1)^p)+(2^p+(p-2)^p)+\cdots}{p}-\frac{p-1}2 $$  Since  $p^2|a^p+(p-a)^p$  for every  $a\in\mathbb{Z}$ , we have  $p^2|(1^p+(p-1)^p)+(2^p+(p-2)^p)+\cdots$ . Then,  $$ LHS=\frac{(1^p+(p-1)^p)+(2^p+(p-2)^p)+\cdots}{p}-\frac{p-1}2\equiv -\frac{p-1}2\equiv \frac{p+1}2\pmod{p} $$  , as desired.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Romania Contests/Other Romanian Contests/Romania - Local Contests/Alexandru Myller/2006 Alexandru Myller/2741537.json

stem_md: For a prime  $ p\ge 5, $  determine the number of polynomials  $ X^p+pX^k+pX^l+1 $  with  $ 1<k<l<p, $  that are ireducible over the integers.
solution_md: The polynomial  $P(X)=X^p+pX^k+pX^l+1$  is irreducible when  $k\equiv l \pmod 2$  (by apply the Eisenstein's criterion on  $P(x-1)$ ) and reducible when  $k\not\equiv l \pmod 2$  (in this case  $(x+1)|P(x)$ ).  The answer to this problem is  $\binom{\frac{p-1}{2}}{2}+\binom{\frac{p-3}{2}}{2}$ .

stem_md: **a)** Show that  $ n^2+2n+2007 $  is squarefree for any natural number  $ n. $ **b)** Prove that for any natural number  $ k\ge 2 $  there is a nonnegative integer  $ m $  such that  $ m^2+2m+2k $  is a perfect square.
solution_md:
Well can we prove that it is never a perfect square?
Yes : $n^2+2n+2007$ is either $ 2$ , either $ 3\pmod 4$ while a perfect square is either $ 0$ , either $ 1\pmod 4$
**b)** Prove that for any natural number $ k\ge 2 $ there is a nonnegative integer $ m $ such that $ m^2+2m+2k $ is a perfect square.
Choose $m=k-2$ for example How did you get to this result?
Just write $m^2+2m+2k=u^2$ as $(u-m-1)(u+m+1)=2k-1$ And splitting $2k-1=\alpha\beta$ , you get for example $m+1=\frac{\alpha-\beta}2$ Choosing $(\alpha,\beta)=(2k-1,1)$ (which always fits even when $2k-1$ is prime, you get $m+1=k-1$
Great Thanks!
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Romania Contests/Other Romanian Contests/Romania - Local Contests/Alexandru Myller/2007 Alexandru Myller/3246322.json

stem_md: Let  $ ABC $  be a right angle in  $ A, $  and  $ M $  be the mid of  $ BC. $  On the perpendicular of  $ AM $  through  $ A $  choose a point  $ D $  so that  $ DM $  meets  $ AB $  at a point, namely  $ P. $  Let  $ E $  be the projection of  $ D $  on  $ BC. $  Show that  $ \angle BPM =\angle EAC. $
solution_md: Since  $\angle MAD = \angle MED = 90 \implies MEDA$  is cyclic, so  $\angle AEM = \angle ADM \implies \angle AEC = \angle ADP$ Also, note that  $\angle DAP = 180 - \angle MAD - \angle BAM = 180 - 90 - \angle ABC = 90 - \angle ABC = \angle ACB$ Thus, in  $\triangle AEC$  and  $\triangle PDA$  we have:  $\angle AEC = \angle ADP$  and  $\angle ACE = \angle DAP$ So, we get  $\angle BPM =\angle EAC$
