stem_md:
There are  $m$  identical rectangular chocolate bars and  $n$  people. Each chocolate bar may be cut into two (possibly unequal) pieces at most once. For which  $m$  and  $n$  is it possible to split the chocolate evenly among all the people?

*Selected from the Kvant Magazine (D. Bugaenko and N. Konstantinov)*
solution_md:
This is the official solution, from Kvant. It is possible if and only if  $m\geqslant n$  or  $m/n=1-1/k$  for some integer  $k\geqslant 2$ .

We begin by showing that these values do work. Let  $\ell$  be the length of the chocolate bars. If  $m\geqslant n$  then place the chocolate bars in a line, forming a rectangle of length  $m\ell$ . Now, simply perform vertical cuts which split this large rectangle into  $n$  equal sections.
[asy]
        size(13cm);
    
        void ho(pair A){filldraw(A--(A+(2,0))--(A+(2,1))--(A+(0,1))--cycle,gray(0.95));}

        ho((-7,0)); ho((-5,0)); ho((-3,0)); ho((-1,0)); ho((1,0)); ho((3,0)); ho((5,0));
    
        draw((7/5,1.25)--(7/5,-0.25), black+dashed); draw((-7/5,1.25)--(-7/5,-0.25), black+dashed);
        
        draw((21/5,1.25)--(21/5,-0.25), black+dashed); draw((-21/5,1.25)--(-21/5,-0.25), black+dashed);
[/asy] 
Because  $m\geqslant n$  the distance between any two cuts is  $m\ell/n\geqslant\ell$  hence each chocolate bar is cut at most once. Now, assume that  $m/n=1-1/k$  for some integer  $k\geqslant 2$ . Observe that in this case,  $k-1$  divides  $m$ . Split the chocolate bars into groups of size  $k-1$ .

Like before, combine the chocolate bars in each group to form a rectangle of length  $\ell(k-1)$  and perform vertical cuts which split each such rectangle into  $k$  equal sections. Thus, we divide the chocolate evenly into  $km/(k-1)=n$  portions. 
    
Note that we cut each chocolate bar at most once. Every chocolate piece created in this manner has length  $t\cdot \ell/k$  for some integer  $t\geqslant 1$ . Thus, if a chocolate bar would be cut at least twice, two of these cuts would be at a distance of at most  $(k-2)\ell/k<(k-1)\ell/k$ , absurd.

Assume that the condition holds for some  $m$  and  $n$  with  $m<n$ . We may also assume, for the sake of simplicity, that each chocolate bar has area one. Then, each person should receive a total area of chocolate equal to  $m/n<1$  so each chocolate bar must be cut. 
    
Suppose that after the cuts, the resulting chocolate pieces have areas  $a_1\leqslant a_2\leqslant\cdots\leqslant a_{2m}.$  Of course, for each  $i$ , the pieces of areas  $a_i$  and  $a_{2m+1-i}$  make up a chocolate bar. We claim that  $a_i/a_1$  is always an integer. We proceed inductively; of course, this holds for  $i=1$ .

Before continuing, observe that  $a_{2m}=m/n$ . If  $a_{2m}>m/n$  then this piece is too large by itself. If  $a_{2m}<m/n$ , then any other piece of chocolate contributes with an area of at least  $a_1$ , which is too much, as  $a_{2m}+a_1=1>m/n$ . Either way, the chocolate cannot be split evenly.

Now, assume that for  $i=1,\ldots,k$  it is true that  $a_i/a_1$  is an integer. Note that since  $a_{k+1}+a_{2m-k}=1>m/n$  then  $a_{2m-k}$  adds up to  $m/n$  with some  $a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_l}<a_{k+1}$ . Hence, the indices  $i_1,\ldots,i_l$  are at most  $k$  so due to the induction,  $(a_{i_1}+\cdots+a_{i_l})/a_1$  is an integer.

Hence, we may write  $a_{2m-k}+t\cdot a_1=m/n$ . Observe further that  $m/n=a_{2m}=1-a_1$  hence we may conclude that  $(t+1)\cdot a_1=1-a_{2m-k}=a_{k+1}$ . Therefore,  $a_{k+1}/a_1$  is an integer too, as desired. This completes the induction.

Now, we may write  $m/n=a_{2m}=(t-1)\cdot a_1$  and  $1=a_{2m}+a_1=t\cdot a_1$  for some integer  $t\geqslant 2$  to infer that  $m/n=1-1/t$ , as we wanted to prove. To conclude, the only  $m$  and  $n$  that work are the ones described above.

stem_md:
Let  $k\geqslant 2$  be a positive integer and  $n>1$  be a composite integer. Let  $d_1<\cdots<d_m$  be all the positive divisors of  $n{}.$  Is it possible for  $d_i+d_{i+1}$  to be a perfect  $k$ -th power, for every  $1\leqslant i<m$ ?

*Proposed by Pavel Ciurea*
solution_md: This was pretty easy unless I fakesolved. The answer is NO. Say there existed a pair $(n,k)$ of positive integers for which this statement holds. Let $p$ be the smallest prime dividing $n$ . We first have the following claim about $n$ . **Claim :**It is not possible to have $d_3 = p^2$ *Proof :* We have that $d_1=1$ and $d_2=p$ . Then, if $d_3=p^2$ , note that \[d_3+d_2=p^2+p=p(p+1)=p(d_2+d_1)\] Now, since by assumption $d_2+d_1$ is a perfect $k$ -th power for $k\geq 2$ , which implies that it is impossible to have $p(d_2+d_1)$ being a perfect $k$ -th power as well ( $\nu_p(p(d_2+d_1))\equiv 1 \pmod{k}$ ). Thus, the only other possibility is $d_3=q$ . In this case note that first, $d_1+d_2$ is a perfect $k$ -th power so let $p+1=r^k$ for some positive integer $r>1$ . Now, we must also have $d_m+d_{m-1}$ being a perfect $k$ -th power so, \[\Tilde{r}^k = n +\frac{n}{p}=\frac{n(p+1)}{p}=\frac{nr^k}{p}\] for some positive integer $\Tilde{r}>1$ . This implies that $n = p \left(\frac{\Tilde{r}}{r}\right)^k$ and thus, $n=ps^k$ for some positive integer $s>1$ . But then, since $d_{m-1}+d_{m-2}$ must also be a perfect $k$ -th power we note that \[\frac{m}{p}+\frac{m}{q}=\frac{m(p+q)}{pq}=\frac{s^kp(p+q)}{pq} = s^k \left(\frac{p+q}{q}\right)\] But now, note that $q \nmid p+q$ and thus, the right hand side of the equality is not an integer while the left hand side is. This is a clear contradiction. Thus, we have exhausted all cases and there indeed this is never possible for any $k\geq 2$ and composite $n$ .

The answer is no. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there exist  $n$  and  $k$  with the desired properties. Observe that  $d_1=1$  and  $d_2=p$ , the smallest prime factor of  $n$ .

Because  $n$  is composite,  $m\geqslant 3$ . Therefore  $d_3$  exists and is either equal to  $p^2$  or some other prime number  $q$ . The former is impossible, because  $p+1$  and  $p(p+1)$  cannot simultaneously be perfect  $k$ -th powers, so  $d_3=q$ , where  $q$  is another prime number.

We may now infer that  $p+1$  and  $p+q$  are perfect  $k$ -th powers. Because  $d_m=n, d_{m-1}=n/p$  and  $d_{m-2}=n/q$  it also follows that  $n(p+1)/p$  and  $n(p+q)/(pq)$  are perfect  $k$ -th powers. This being said,  $n/p$  and  $n/(pq)$  must simultaneously be perfect  $k$ -th powers, which is absurd.

stem_md:
We are given an infinite set of points in the plane such that any two of them have a distance of at most one. Prove that all the axes of symmetry of this set are concurrent, provided that there are at least two of them. 

*Proposed by David Anghel*
solution_md:
Let  $\ell_1{}$  and  $\ell_2{}$  be two axes of symmetry. First, we prove that they are not parallel.

Assume the contrary, so  $\ell_1{}$  and  $\ell_2{}$  are parallel. Suppose further that they are also parallel to the  $x{}$ -axis, having  $y{}$ -coordinates  $a$  and  $b$ . Thus, if a point  $P_0=(c,d)$  is in the set, then its reflection  $P_1{}$  in  $\ell_1{}$  belongs to the set and the reflection  $P_2{}$  of  $P_1{}$  in  $\ell_2{}$  also belongs to the set. 
    
Observe that  $P_2=(c,2(a-b)+d)$  and  $a\neq b$ . Thus, we can continue to perform this procedure, so for any positive integer  $n$ , the point  $P_{2n}=(c,2n(a-b)+d)$  belongs to the set. This eventually yields a contradiction, distance-wise.

To conclude,  $\ell_1{}$  and  $\ell_2{}$  meet at some point  $P{}$ . Consider some other axis of symmetry  $\ell{}$  and assume that it does not pass through  $P{}$ . Let  $d=\text{dist}(P,\ell)$  and consider an arbitrary point  $X$  from the set. We may now prove the main claim.**Claim.** There exists a point  $Y$  in the set, such that  $PY^2\geqslant PX^2+4d^2$ .

*Proof.* Let  $\ell'$  be the parallel to  $\ell$  passing through  $P$ . A reflection in  $\ell_1{}$  combined with a reflection in  $\ell_2{}$  is a rotation with the pivot in  $P$ . By eventually considering the reverse procedure, we may assume that the angle of this rotation is at most  $\pi$ . 

Evidently, the angle of rotation is non-zero, because  $\ell_1\neq\ell_2$ . Therefore, we can repeatedly apply this rotation on  $X$  until we get a point  $X'$  which satisfies  $PX=PX'$  and which is not on the same side of  $\ell'{}$  as  $\ell{}$ . Take  $Y$  to be the reflection of  $X'$  in  $\ell$ .

Note that  $X'Y$  is perpendicular to  $\ell$ . Let  $Z=X'Y\cap\ell$ . By Pythagoras' theorem, we have\[PY^2-PX'^2=PZ^2+YZ^2-PZ^2-X'Z^2=(YZ-X'Z)(YZ+X'Z).\]As  $YZ-X'Z=2d$  and  $X'Z\geqslant 0$ , we get the desired inequality.  $\square$ To see why the claim finishes the problem, take an arbitrary point  $A_0$  from the set, and use the claim inductively to prove the existence of a point  $A_n$  from the set, such that  $PA_n^2\geqslant PA_0^2 +4nd^2.$  Therefore, \[1+PA_0\geqslant A_0A_n+ PA_0\geqslant PA_n \geqslant 2d\sqrt{n},\] a contradiction for large enough  $n$ .**Remark.** If there are at least three axes of symmetry, one may give an alternative solution which makes use of the following property: given a triangle  $\Delta$ , for an adequate ordering  $a,b,c$  of its sides, the series of reflections in  $a,b,c,a,b,c$  produces a non-trivial translation.

The proof consists of computations with the aid of complex numbers, so we will not present it.

stem_md:
On the surface of a sphere, a non-intersecting closed curve is drawn. It divides the surface of the sphere in two regions, which are coloured red and blue. Prove that there exist two antipodes of different colours. *Note: the curve is colourless.*

*Proposed by Vlad Spătaru*
solution_md:
I hope this is correct.

Suppose not. Let  $p \colon S^2 \to \mathbb{RP}^2$  be the cover identifying antipodes, and let  $R$  denote the red region. Observe that


- $R$  is homeomorphic to the open disk  $D^2$  by the Jordan Curve Theorem,
- The restriction  $p|_R \colon R \to p(R)$  is a double cover of  $p(R)$  by  $R$  because the antipode of a red point is red (there is a bit of work to show that it can't be colorless, but you can basically achieve a contradiction by considering a small open ball centered at the point and inside  $R$ ),
- Any cover by  $D^2$  is a homeomorphism because it would have to be a universal cover, but then Brouwer's Fixed Point Theorem implies that the group of deck transformations is trivial.

This is a contradiction.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
Find all the functions  $\varphi:\mathbb{Z}[x]\to\mathbb{Z}[x]$  such that  $\varphi(x)=x,$  any integer polynomials  $f, g$  satisfy  $\varphi(f+g)=\varphi(f)+\varphi(g)$  and  $\varphi(f)$  is a perfect power if and only if  $f{}$  is a perfect power.

*Note:* A polynomial  $f\in \mathbb{Z}[x]$  is a perfect power if  $f = g^n$  for some  $g\in \mathbb{Z}[x]$  and  $n\geqslant 2.$ *Proposed by Pavel Ciurea*
solution_md:
We can in fact characterize all additive functions on  $\mathbb{Z}[x]$  preserving perfect powers. We will need to lemmas:**Lemma 1:** Let  $P\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$  such that  $P(a)$  is an integer perfect power for all  $a\in\mathbb{Z}$ . Then there exists some  $Q\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$  and  $k\geq 2$  such that  $P=Q^k$ , i.e.  $P$  is itself a perfect power.**Lemma 2:** If  $P\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$  is nonconstant and irreducible,  $Q,R\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$  nonconstant and  $k\geq 2$  s.t.  $P(Q(x))=R^k$ , then  $P=ax+b$  with  $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ ,  $a\neq 0$ , and thus  $Q=\frac{R^k-b}{a}$ .

The first one is rather well-known (for reference, check out the stronger version from [url =https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c833908h2097762p15169303]USMCA 2020[/url]). The proof of the second one is rather straight-forward.
Differentiating yields  $P'(Q(x))Q'(x)=kR^{k-1}R'$  implying  $P'(Q(x))Q'(x)R(x)=kP(Q(x))R'(x)$ . Since  $P$  is irreducible,  $\gcd(P,P')=1$ , so (by Bezout for instance)  $\gcd(P(Q),P'(Q))=1$ , implying that  $P'(Q(x))\mid R'(x)$ , so  $(\deg P-1)\deg Q\leq \deg R-1$ . However,  $\deg P\deg Q = k\deg R$ , so replacing  $\deg R$  above,  $\deg P<\frac{k}{k-1}\leq 2$ , implying that  $P=ax+b$ . (Throughout the proof we worked in  $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ .)

Now, returning to the problem, notice that  $\varphi(m^n)=m^n\varphi(1)$ . Thus if we take  $m$  coprime with  $c(\varphi(1))$  (the content of  $\varphi(1)$ ) and  $n$  prime,  $\varphi(1)$  will be an  $n^{\text{th}}$  power. Since this is true for all primes  $n$ ,  $\varphi(1)=1$  ( $\varphi(1)\neq 0$ , otherwise  $\varphi(2)=0$  which is a perfect power, however  $2$  isn't).

Now suppose we have shown that  $\varphi(x^k)=\varphi^k(x)$  for all  $k\leq n-1$ ,  $n\geq 2$ . Then   $$ \varphi((x+a)^n)=\varphi\left(\sum_{k=0}^n x^ka^{n-k}\binom{n}{k}\right)=\sum_{k=0}^n\varphi(x^k)a^{n-k}\binom{n}{k}=\varphi(x^n)-\varphi^n(x)+(\varphi(x)+a)^n. $$   For a fixed integer  $x$ , consider the RHS as a polynomial in  $a$ . Notice the LHS is a perfect power, so for every integer  $a$ , the RHS is an integer perfect power, implying by Lemma 1 that   $$ (\varphi(x)+a)^n+\varphi(x^n)-\varphi^n(x)=P^k(a) $$   where  $k\geq 2$ ,  $P\in\mathbb{Z}[a]$  and the coefficients of  $P$  depend on  $x$ . Inspecting degrees,  $k\mid n$ , so write  $n=kl$ . Thus, for large enough  $a$ ,   $$ ((\varphi(x)+a)^l-1)^k<(\varphi(x)+a)^n+\varphi(x^n)-\varphi^n(x)<((\varphi(x)+a)^l+1)^k, $$   implying that  $P(a)=(\varphi(x)+a)^l$ , so  $\varphi(x^n)=\varphi^n(x)$ .

Inductively, we have shown that  $\varphi(x^n)=\varphi^n(x)$  for all  $n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , so  $\varphi(P)=P(\varphi(x))$ . Denote  $\varphi(x)=Q$ . We are now in search of the polynomials  $Q\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$  s.t.  $P(Q)$  is a perfect power iff  $P$  is a perfect power.

Suppose  $Q$  is nonconstant. Otherwise, if  $Q=c$ , then  $P=x-c$  is not a perfect power, and yet  $P(Q)=0$  which is.
Decompose  $P=c^{\alpha_0}\prod_{i=1}^n P_i^{\alpha_i}$  into irreducible factors. Thus  $P(Q)=c^{\alpha_0}\prod_{i=1}^n P_i(Q)^{\alpha_i}$ . If  $P(Q)$  were to be a perfect power and  $P$  not, since  $P_i(Q)$  are all coprime, the factors  $P_i(Q)^{\alpha_i}$  would all have to be  $k^{\text{th}}$  powers for some  $k\geq 2$ , and since the  $\alpha_i$  are all coprime, one of the polynomials  $P_i(Q)$  must be a perfect power. By Lemma 2, this implies that  $Q$  is some  $R^k$  scaled and/or translated. Of course (as it can be seen from the proof of Lemma 2), if  $Q$  is of that form, there is an irreducible  $P$  s.t.  $P(Q)$  is a perfect power, and obviously  $P$  isn't.

To sum things up, all additive functions  $\varphi$  on  $\mathbb{Z}[x]$  preserving perfect powers are exactly the ones of the form  $\varphi(P(x))=P(Q(x))$  for some  $Q\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$  not of the form  $\frac{R^k-b}{a}$ .

stem_md:
Let  $ABC$  be an acute scalene triangle with orthocentre  $H{}$  and circumcentre  $O.{}$  Let  $P{}$  be an arbitrary point on the segment  $OH$  and  $O_a$  be the circumcentre of  $PBC.{}$  The line  $PO_a$  intersects the line  $HA$  at  $X_a.{}$  Define  $X_b$  and  $X_c$  similarly. Let  $Q{}$  be the isogonal conjugate of  $P{}$  and  $X{}$  be the circumcentre of  $X_aX_bX_c.{}$  Prove that  $PQ$  and  $HX$  are parallel.

*Proposed by David Anghel*
solution_md:
Very nice problem! I might clean this solution up at some point.**Claim.** The homothety with center  $P$  and ratio  $-\frac{HP}{HO}$  maps  $X_aX_bX_c\cup X$  to  $O_aO_bO_c\cup O$ .**Proof.** Simply notice that  $OO_a\parallel AH$ , so  $\frac{HP}{HO}=\frac{PX_a}{PO_a}$ . Our claim follows due to the similar ratio equalities.

Let  $K$  be the circumcenter of  $O_aO_bO_c$ . Then due to our claim (because the image of  $X$  under the homothety is  $K$ ) we have  $HX\parallel OK$ , so the desired reduces to showing that  $OK\parallel PQ$ .

We now considered the homothety  $\mathcal{H}$  with center  $P$  and ratio  $1/2$ . Since  $O_bO_c$  is the perpendicular bisector of  $AP$ , it follows that  $\mathcal{H}\left(A\right)=A'$ , the projection of  $A$  onto  $O_bO_c$ . Define  $B'$  and  $C'$  similarly.

Let  $\mathcal{H}\left(O\right)=O'$  be the circumcenter of  $\triangle A'B'C'$  and let  $\mathcal{H}\left(Q\right)=Q'$  be the isogonal conjugate of  $P$  in  $\triangle A'B'C'$ . Finally, let  $\mathcal{H}\left(K\right)=M$  be the midpoint of  $PK$ .

The conclusion then reduces to showing that  $MO'\parallel PQ'$ . If we let  $X$  be the projection of  $Q'$  onto  $B'C'$  and define  $Y$  and  $Z$  similarly, the crux of the problem is the following claim.**Claim.**  $\triangle XYZ$  and  $\triangle O_aO_bO_c$  are homothetic under a homothety  $\mathcal{H}'$ .**Proof.** We show that  $YZ\parallel O_bO_c$ , which suffices. Notice that  $$ \angle PA'Y=\angle QA'Z=90^{\circ}-\angle A'QZ=90^{\circ}-\angle A'YZ, $$  so  $PA\perp YZ$ . However  $PA\perp O_bO_c$ , so the desired follows.**Claim.** Let  $S$  be the isogonal conjugate of  $P$  in  $\triangle O_aO_bO_c$ . Then  $\mathcal{H}'\left(Q'\right)=S$ .**Proof.** We show that  $O_aS\parallel XQ'$ , which suffices. Note that  $$ \angle SO_aB'=\angle PO_aC'=\angle PB'C'=\angle Q'B'Z=\angle Q'XZ, $$  so since  $XZ\parallel O_aO_c$ , it follows that  $O_aS\parallel XQ'$  indeed.

Since  $P$  and  $S$  are isogonal conjugates in  $\triangle O_aO_bO_c$  and  $\triangle A'B'C'$  is the pedal triangle of  $P$  in  $\triangle O_aO_bO_c$ , it follows that  $O'$  is the midpoint of  $PS$ .

Because  $P$  and  $Q'$  are isogonal conjugates in  $\triangle A'B'C'$  and  $\triangle XYZ$  is the pedal triangle of  $Q'$  in  $\triangle A'B'C'$ , it follows that  $P$  is the reflection of  $Q'$  across the circumcenter  $O''$  of  $\triangle XYZ$ .

Then  $\mathcal{H}'\left(P\right)=P'$  is the reflection of  $\mathcal{H}'\left(Q'\right)=S$  across  $\mathcal{H}'\left(O''\right)=K$ . Thus because  $\mathcal{H'}\left(Q'\right)=S$  and  $\mathcal{H'}\left(P\right)=P'$  we have  $PQ'\parallel SP'$ , so the desired reduces to showing that  $MO'\parallel SP'$ . But  $M$  is the midpoint of  $PK$  and  $O'$  is the midpoint of  $PS$ , so  $MO'\parallel SK$  or equivalently  $MO'\parallel SP'$ , ending our proof.

stem_md: Let  $n\geqslant 2$  be an integer. Prove that for any positive real numbers  $a_1, a_2,\ldots, a_n$ , \[\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}2^{i}a_i^2 \geqslant\sum_{1 \leqslant i < j \leqslant n}a_i a_j.\]*Proposed by Andrei Vila*
solution_md:
We prove the inequality by inducting on  $n$ . For  $n=2$ , the base case, the inequality is equivalent to  $a_1^2+2a_2^2\geqslant\sqrt{2}a_1a_2$  which is true by the am-gm inequality. Now, assume that the inequality is true for some integer  $n\geqslant 2$ . 

We will prove it also holds for  $n+1$ . By applying the inequality for the  $n$  terms  $a_2,\ldots,a_{n+1}$  it follows that \[\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\sum_{i=2}^{n+1}2^{i-1}a_i^2\geqslant\sum_{2\leqslant i<j\leqslant n+1}a_ia_j.\]Therefore, in order to prove the general inequality for  $n+1$ , it suffices to show that \[\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\left(2a_1^2+\sum_{i=2}^{n+1}2^{i-1}a_i^2\right)\geqslant a_1(a_2+\cdots+a_{n+1}).\]One may easily observe that  $2\geqslant 2^0+2^{-1}+\cdots+2^{-(n-1)}$ . The latter inequality then follows as such:\[\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\left(2a_1^2+\sum_{i=2}^{n+1}2^{i-1}a_i^2\right)\geqslant\sum_{i=2}^{n+1}\frac{2^{-(i-2)}a_1^2+2^{i-1}a_i^2}{2\sqrt{2}}\geqslant\sum_{i=2}^{n+1}a_1a_i,\]by applying the am-gm inequality on each term.**Remark 1.** More generally, with the same approach, one can prove that \[y\sum_{i=1}^nx^ia_i^2\geqslant\sum_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant n}a_ia_j,\]provided that  $x>1$  and  $2y(x-1)\geqslant1/\sqrt{x}$ . In the problem above, we used  $x=2$  and  $y=1/2\sqrt{2}$ .**Remark 2.** We present another possible approach. The inequality is equivalent to \[\sum_{i=1}^n \left(1+\frac{2^i}{\sqrt{2}}\right)a_i^2\geqslant \left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)^2,\]which is true by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, because\[\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{1+2^i/\sqrt{2}}<\sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{1}{1+2^i/\sqrt{2}}\approx0.9927<1.\]

stem_md:
Let  $n$  be a positive integer. Consider an infinite checkered board. A set  $S$  of cells is *connected* if one may get from any cell in  $S$  to any other cell in  $S$  by only traversing edge-adjacent cells in  $S$ . Find the largest integer  $k_n$  with the following property: in any connected set with  $n$  cells, one can find  $k_n$  disjoint pairs of adjacent cells (that is,  $k_n$  disjoint dominoes).

*Proposed by David Anghel and Vlad Spătaru*
solution_md: Solution during contest: The answer is $\boxed {\lceil \frac{n-1}{4} \rceil}$ We need the following lemma: Lemma: Let $G$ be a connected graph with n vertices and $deg v\le 4$ for every $v$ .Then you can find $\lceil \frac{n-1}{4} \rceil$ disjoint edges. Proof: induction $\blacksquare$ Obviously our problem is just a graph with above properties and so we can find $\lceil \frac{n-1}{4} \rceil$ dominoes. Example is just putting $k$ verices as centers and then draw $4$ neighbours such that any two neghbouring centers have a common neighbour(to ensure connectivity)

stem_md: Let  $p$  be a prime number and  $\mathcal{A}$  be a finite set of integers, with at least  $p^k$  elements. Denote by  $N_{\text{even}}$  the number of subsets of  $\mathcal{A}$  with even cardinality and sum of elements divisible by  $p^k$ . Define  $N_{\text{odd}}$  similarly. Prove that  $N_{\text{even}}\equiv N_{\text{odd}}\bmod{p}.$
solution_md:
This is the first official solution, translated in English. It is technical, but instructive. The second official solution is much trickier to find, but very beautiful. I certainly recommend giving it a read.

Let  $\mathcal{A}=\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}$  with  $n\geqslant p^k$ . We will encode each subset of  $\mathcal{A}$  as an  $n$ -digit code  $(\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_n)$  where  $\chi_i=1$  if  $a_i$  belongs to the subset and  $\chi_i=0$  otherwise. Evidently, the sum of elements of the subset is  $\chi_1a_1+\cdots+\chi_na_n.$     
We will construct an  $n$ -variable polynomial  $f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$  with integer coefficients, whose degree does not exceed  $p^k-1$  and which satisfies \[f(\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_n)\equiv\begin{cases}1\bmod p & \text{if } p^k\mid \chi_1a_1+\cdots+\chi_na_n; 0\bmod p &\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\tag{ $\dagger$ }\]for any  $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_n\in\{0,1\}$ . To exhibit a construction, we will consider a sequence of monomials. The term  $x_1$  is written  $a_1$  times, followed by  $x_2$  written  $a_2$  times and so on, ending with  $x_n$  written  $a_n$  times and the constant  $1$  written  $p^k-1$  times:\[(\underbrace{x_1,\ldots,x_1}_{a_1\text{ times}},\underbrace{x_2,\ldots,x_2}_{a_2\text{ times}},\ldots,\underbrace{x_n,\ldots,x_n}_{a_n\text{ times}},\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{p^k-1\text{ times}}),\]for a total of  $N:=a_1+\cdots+a_n+p^k-1$  monomials. Then, for each  $1\leqslant i\leqslant N$ , let  $g_i(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$  be the  $i$ -th term of this monomial sequence. Consider every  $(p^k-1)$ -tuple of polynomials of the form  $g_i$ , take their product and sum everything in order to get\[f(x_1,\ldots,x_n):=\sum
    g_{i_1}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\cdots g_{i_{p^k-1}}(x_1,\ldots,x_n),\]for every  $1\leqslant i_1<\cdots<i_{p^k-1}\leqslant N$ . Evidently, this polynomial has degree  $d\leqslant p^k-1$ . Moreover, given any  $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_n\in\{0,1\}$ , then there are precisely  $\chi_1a_1+\cdots+\chi_na_n+p^k-1$  ones among the numbers  $g_i(\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_n)$  so\[f(\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_n)\equiv\binom{\chi_1a_1+\cdots+\chi_na_n+p^k-1}{p^k-1}\bmod{p},\]which satisfies the congruence  $(\dagger)$  due to Lucas' theorem. This construction is satisfactory. 
    
Let  $C_{u_1,\ldots,u_n}$  be the coefficient of the term  $x_1^{u_1}\cdots x_n^{u_n}$  in the expansion of  $f$ . For the sake of brevity, in what follows, any instance of  $\chi_i$  will denote a number in  $\{0,1\}.$  The main observation is\[N_{\text{even}}-N_{\text{odd}}\equiv\sum_{\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_n}(-1)^{\chi_1+\cdots+\chi_n}f(\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_n)\bmod{p}.\]We will denote  $\chi_1+\cdots+\chi_n$  by  $\Sigma\chi_i$ . Observe that the right-hand side is equal to\begin{align*}\sum_{\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_n}(-1)^{\Sigma\chi_i}\sum_{u_1,\ldots,u_n}C_{u_1,\ldots,u_n}\chi_1^{u_1}\cdots\chi_n^{u_n}&=\sum_{u_1,\ldots,u_n}C_{u_1,\ldots,u_n}\sum_{\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_n}(-1)^{\Sigma\chi_i}\chi_1^{u_1}\cdots\chi_n^{u_n}  &=\sum_{u_1,\ldots,u_n}C_{u_1,\ldots,u_n}\prod_{i=1}^n\left(\sum_{\chi_i\in\{0,1\}}(-1)^{\chi_i}\chi_i^{u_i}\right).\end{align*}Because  $\deg f<p^k\leqslant n$  then among every  $u_1,\ldots,u_n$  there exists at least one index  $i$  such that  $u_i=0$ , hence the right-hand side is equal to zero, as desired.

stem_md:
Find all functions  $f:\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$  with the following properties:
1) For every natural number  $n\geq 3$ ,  $\gcd(f(n),n)\neq 1$ .
2) For every natural number  $n\geq 3$ , there exists  $i_n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ ,  $1\leq i_n\leq n-1$ , such that  $f(n)=f(i_n)+f(n-i_n)$ .

*Proposed by Pavel Ciurea*
solution_md:
Let  $f(1)=a,f(2)=b$ Then  $f(3)=a+b$ Now by induction not hard to prove, that  $f(2n)$  is in form  $2k*a+(n-k)*b$  for some  $0 \leq k \leq n-1$  and  $f(2n+1)$  is in form   $(2k+1)*a+(n-k)*b$ Take such  $n$  that  $2n+1$  is prime
Then  $2n+1| (2k+1)a+(n-k)b \to 2n+1 | (4k+2)a+(2n+1-2k-1)b \to 2n+1 | (4k+2)a-(2k+1)b=(2k+1)(2a-b)$  and as  $k<n$  then it means that  $2n+1|2a-b$  for every prime  $2n+1$ But it is possible only if  $b=2a$ So  $f(1)=a,f(2)=2a$  and  $f(n)=n*a$

stem_md:
Let  $ABC$  be a triangle and  $P$  a point in its interior. Circle  $\Gamma_A$  is considered such that it is tangent to rays  $(PB$  and  $(PC$ . Define similarly  $\Gamma_B$  and  $\Gamma_C$ . Let  $\ell_A\neq PA$  be the other common internal tangent of  $\Gamma_B$  and  $\Gamma_C$ . Prove that  $\ell_A$ ,  $\ell_B$  and  $\ell_C$  meet at a point.

*Proposed by Andrei Vila*
solution_md:
Let  $X,Y,Z$  are the center of  $\Gamma_A,\Gamma_B,\Gamma_C$ ,respectively. $PA$  meets  $\ell_A$  at  $D$ ,then  $D$  lies on the  $YZ$ , $E,F$  similarly.
It is known that there is a ellipse tangent  $YZ,ZX,XY$  at  $D,E,F$ ,respectively.
And by  $\angle FPX=\angle EPX,\angle FPY=\angle DPY,\angle DPZ=\angle EPZ$ ,we can know that  $P$  is a focal-point of this ellipse.
Consider another focal-point of this ellipse  $Q$ ,we can know  $\angle YDP=\angle ZDQ$  and similarly for  $E,F$ .
So  $\ell_A,\ell_B,\ell_C$  all pass  $Q$ . $\Box$ .

stem_md:
Let  $a_1<a_2 \dots <a_n$  be positive integers, with  $n\geq 2$ . An invisible frog lies on the real line, at a positive integer point. Initially, the hunter chooses a number  $k$ , and then, once every minute, he can check if the frog currently lies in one of  $k$  points of his choosing, after which the frog goes from its point  $x$  to one of the points  $x+a_1, x+a_2 \dots x+a_n$ . Based on the values of  $a_1, a_2 \dots a_n$ , what is the smallest value of  $k$  such that the hunter can guarantee to find the frog within a finite number of minutes, no matter where it initially started?

*Proposed by David Anghel*
solution_md: The frog wants to go far behind from the hunter. So it will move  $x+a_i$  where  $a_i$  is  $\max \left\{a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots, a_n\right\}$ . Now, if the hunter's chosen number  $(k)$  is less or equal to  $\max \left\{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\right\}$  then for every position of frog (initial) ie.  $x>\max \left\{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\right\}$  the hunter can't catch the frog. So the minimum value of  $k$  is  $\max \left\{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\right\}+1$ . After some finite number of moves, the extra one move made by the hunter will become  $x+1$ . Then the frog will be caught.

stem_md: Find all functions  $f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ , such that for any real numbers  $x,y$  with  $y\neq 0$  we have   $$ f(f(x)+y)f\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)=xf\left(\frac{1}{y}\right) + 1. $$  *Proposed by Marius Cerlat*
solution_md:
Find all functions $f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ , such that for any real numbers $x,y$ with $y\neq 0$ we have $$ f(f(x)+y)f\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)=xf\left(\frac{1}{y}\right) + 1. $$
Let $P(x,y)$ be the assertion $f(f(x)+y)f(\frac 1y)=xf(\frac 1y)+1$ If $f(f(x))\ne x$ for some $x$ , then $P(f(x),x-f(f(x)))$ $\implies$ contradiction. So $f(f(x))=x$ $\forall x$ and $f(x)$ is bijective Let $u=f^{-1}(0)$ : $P(u,x)$ $\implies$ $f(x)f(\frac 1x)=uf(\frac 1x)+1$ $\forall x\ne 0$ Moving there $x\to \frac 1x$ and subtracting, we get $u(f(x)-f(\frac 1x))=0$ $\forall x\ne 0$ and so, since injective, $u=0$ And two lines above becomes $f(x)f(\frac 1x)=1$ $\forall x\ne 0$ Multiplying then $P(x,y)$ both sides by $f(y)$ , we get $f(f(x)+y)=x+f(y)$ And so, moving $x\to f(x)$ , $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ $\forall x$ , $\forall y\ne 0$ , still true when $y=0$ This implies $f(x+\frac 1x)=f(x)+\frac 1{f(x)}$ and so graph of $f(x)$ has no point in $[2,+\infty)\times (-2,+2)$ So $f(x)$ is linear (since graph of non linear additive functions is dense in $\mathbb R^2$ ) and only two solutions : $\boxed{\text{S1 : }f(x)=x\quad\forall x}$ , which indeed fits $\boxed{\text{S2 : }f(x)=-x\quad\forall x}$ , which indeed fits

stem_md: Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integers  $d$  such that we can find a polynomial  $P\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$  of degree  $d$  and  $N\in\mathbb{N}$  such that for all integers  $x>N$  and any prime  $p$ , we have   $$ \nu_p(P(x)^3+3P(x)^2-3)<\frac{d\cdot\log(x)}{2024^{2024}}. $$  *Proposed by Marius Cerlat*
solution_md:
Solution during contest:
First, note that for any prime  $p$  and  $n \in \mathbb{N}$  we have  $v_p(n) \leq \log_p(n)=\frac{\ln(n)}{\ln(p)}$ .
The plan is to construct a polynomial which works for all sufficiently small primes, as the others work basically "by default".
To this end, consider the polynomial  $P(X)=X^d$ , where we take  $d$  to be of the form  $k\prod_{p \le e^{6 \cdot 2024^{2024}}}(p-1)$  for some  $k\in \mathbb{N}$ , the product being taken over the primes  $p$ .
For sufficiently large  $X$ , we have  $v_p(P(X)^3+3P(X)^2-3) \le \log_p(2P(X)^3) = \log_p(2) + \log_p(X^{3d}) = \log_p(2)+\frac{3d\ln(X)}{\ln(p)}$ For primes  $p>e^{6 \cdot 2024^{2024}}$ ,  $\log_p(2)+\frac{3d\ln(X)}{\ln(p)}$  is clearly less than  $\frac{d\ln(X)}{2024^{2024}}$  for sufficiently large  $X$ .
Now we are left with the primes  $p\le e^{6 \cdot 2024^{2024}}$ .
For such a prime  $p$ ,  $p-1|d$ . Thus for  $x\in \mathbb{N}$  with  $\gcd(x, p)=1$ : $ord_p(x)|p-1|d \implies x^d \equiv 1$  (mod  $p$ ), so  $v_p(P(x)^3+3P(x)^2-3)=0$  and we are done in this case.
If  $x \equiv 0$  (mod  $p$ ): $P(x)^3+3P(x)^2-3\equiv -3$  (mod  $p$ )
It is clear that we are done if  $p\neq 3$ . Finally, for  $p=3$ : $9|P(x)^3$  and  $9|3P(x)^2$ , so  $P(x)^3+3P(x)^2-3 \equiv 6$  (mod  $9$ ).
Therefore  $v_3(P(x)^3+3P(x)^2-3)=1$  which is clearly less than  $\frac{d\ln x}{2024^{2024}}$  for sufficiently large  $x$ .
In conclusion, all cases having been covered, the provided polynomial satisfies the conditions. 
By letting  $k$  run over the natural numbers in our choice of  $d$ , we find an infinity of positive integers  $d$  for which there exists a suitable polynomial.

stem_md:
On a table, there are  $2025$  empty boxes numbered  $1,2,\dots ,2025$ , and  $2025$  balls with weights  $1,2,\dots ,2025$ . Starting with Vadim, Vadim and Marian take turns selecting a ball from the table and placing it into an empty box. After all  $2025$  turns, there is exactly one ball in each box. Denote the weight of the ball in box  $i$  by  $w_i$ . Marian wins if   $$ \sum_{i=1}^{2025}i\cdot w_i\equiv 0 \pmod{23}. $$   If both players play optimally, can Marian guarantee a win?

*Proposed by Pavel Ciurea*
solution_md:
No, Marian doesn't have a winning strategy.
Vadim can obtain  $\sum_{i=1}^{2025}i\cdot w_i\equiv 1 \pmod{23}$ , independently of the Marian's moves. $2025=88\cdot23+1$ .
Hence, the set of the first  $2025$  natural numbers contains: $\bullet\quad88 $  numbers  $a$ , with  $23|a$ ; $\bullet\quad89 $  numbers  $b$ , with  $b\equiv 1 \pmod{23}$ ; $\bullet\quad88 $  numbers  $c$ , with  $c\equiv k \pmod{23}$ , for each  $k\in\{2,3,...,21,22\}$ .

In the first turn, Vadim selects the ball with weight  $1$  and places it into the box numbered  $1$ . Results the first term in the requested sum:  $1\cdot w_1=1$ .

Next, we will use all operations using modulo  $23$ : $\bullet$   we replace  $n$  (the number of a box or the weight of a ball) with  $n\pmod{23}$ ; $\bullet$   we replace  $x+y$  with  $(x+y)\pmod{23}$ ; $\bullet$   we replace  $xy$  with  $xy\pmod{23}$ ; $\bullet$   we replace  $-y$  with  $-y\pmod{23}$ .

Using these conventions, after Vadim's first move remain exactly  $88$  boxes numbered  $n$  and exactly  $88$  balls with the weight  $n$ , for each  $n\in\{0,1,2,...,21,22\}$ .

If in a turn Marian puts in a box  $x$  a ball with the weight  $y$ , in the next turn Vadim puts in a box  $x$  a ball with the weight  $-y$ . Corresponding to these  $2$  turns, we obtain a partial sum, as part of the requested sum,  $x\cdot y+x\cdot(-y)=0$ .
The Vadim's move is always possible, since after  $2m-1$  turns,  $m\in\{1,2,...,1011,1012\}$ : $\bullet$  remains an even number of boxes numbered  $x$ ; $\bullet$  remains an even number of balls with the weight  $0$ ; $\bullet$  the number of the balls with the weight  $y$  is equal to the number of the balls with the weight  $-y,\;\forall y\in\{1,2,...,21,22\}$ . $\textbf{Conclusions:}$  $\bullet$  the sum  $\sum_{i=2}^{2025}i\cdot w_i\equiv0\pmod{23}$ , as sum of  $1012$  expressions of the form  $x\cdot y+x\cdot(-y)$ . $\bullet\quad\sum_{i=1}^{2025}i\cdot w_i=1\cdot w_1+\sum_{i=2}^{2025}i\cdot w_i\equiv1\pmod{23}$ .

stem_md:
Let  $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ ,  $n\geq 2$ . Find all functions  $f:\mathbb{R}_{>0}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{>0}$  such that   $$ f(x_1+\dots +x_n)^2=\sum_{i=1}^nf(x_i) ^2+ 2\sum_{i<j}f(x_ix_j), $$   for all  $x_1,\dots ,x_n\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ .

*Proposed by Andrei Vila*
solution_md:
Cute but standard.

Let  $P(x_1,x_2, \dots, x_n)$  denote the given FE.  $P(x,y,y,\dots,y)$  gives  $f(x+(n-1)y)^2=f(x)^2+(n-1)^2f(y)^2+2(n-1)f(xy)$ , or, letting  $z=(n-1)y$ , we get   $$ f(x+z)^2=f(x)^2+2(n-1)f\left(\frac{xz}{n-1}\right)+(n-1)^2f\left(\frac{z}{n-1}\right)^2. $$  Switching  $x,z$  in the above and comparing, we get  $f(x)^2-(n-1)^2f\left(\frac{x}{n-1}\right)^2=c$  for some constant  $c$ , for all  $x>0$ . Putting this in the above equation gives  $f(x+z)^2=f(x)^2+2\sqrt{f(xz)^2-c}+f(z)^2-c$  for all  $x,z>0$ . Let  $g(x)=\sqrt{f(x)^2-c}$ ; then  $g(x+z)^2=g(x)^2+2g(xz)+g(z)^2$  for all  $x,z>0$ . Call this  $Q(x,z)$ .

Now,  $Q(x+t,y)$  followed by  $Q(x,t)$  gives   $$ g(x+y+t)^2=g(x)^2+g(y)^2+g(t)^2+2g(xt)+2g(xy+yt) $$  for all  $x,y,t>0$ . Switching  $x,y$  and comparing gives  $g(xt)+g(xy+yt)=g(yt)+g(xy+xt)$  for all  $x,y,t>0$ . Now for any  $a,b>0$  with  $a<b$ , we can find  $x,y,t$  such that  $xt=a$ ,  $yt=\frac{a+b}{2}$ , and  $xy=\frac{b-a}{2}$ ; indeed take their product and square root to get  $xyt$ , and solve individually for  $x,y,t$ . Putting this in the above equation, we get  $g(a)+g(b)=2g\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)$ , and this clearly also holds when  $a=b$ . Thus  $g$  satisfies Jensen's FE over  $\mathbb{R}^+$ , and it is well known that the only solutions are of the form  $g(x)=dx+e$  for some  $d>0$  and  $e \geq 0$ . Plugging in  $Q(x,y)$ , we see that we must have  $e=0$  and  $d=1$ . Putting this for  $f$  gives  $f(x)=\sqrt{x^2+c}$ . However  $f$  also satisfies  $f(x)^2-(n-1)^2f\left(\frac{x}{n-1}\right)^2=c$  for all  $x>0$ , and equating this gives  $c(1-(n-1)^2)=c$ , which is only possible if  $c=0$ . Thus we get  $$ \boxed{f(x)=x \ \ \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^+} $$  which clearly is a solution.

A circle  $\omega$  with center  $Q$  is internally tangent to  $\Omega$  at  $A$ , and touches segment  $BC$ . If the circle with diameter  $IM$  meets  $\Omega$  again at  $J$ , prove that  $JI$  bisects  $\angle QJN$ .

stem_md:
Find all positive integers  $n$  such that  $$ 1^n + 2^n + \dots + n^n $$  is a prime number.

*Proposed by Marius Cerlat*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Boiled down to finite checking</summary>We'll use the famous result of  $1^x + \cdots + (p-1)^x \equiv -1 \pmod p$  if  $p-1 \mid x$  otherwise it is  $0\pmod p$ . Let some odd prime  $p\mid n$ , write  $n=p\cdot k$  using the fact that  $a^n \equiv a^k \pmod p$  the sum \[S \equiv k(1^k + \cdots + p^k) \pmod p\]
if  $p\mid k$  then  $p \mid S$  which is not possible, if  $p-1 \nmid k$  then  $p \mid S$  but clearly  $S>p$  so it cannot be prime, so we must have  $p-1 \mid k$ . Notice that  $4 \mid n$  does not work by reducing  $\pmod 2$  so we can write  $n = 2 \cdot p_1\cdots p_m$  where  $2 < p_1 <\cdots < p_m$ . Now  $p_1 -1 \mid n$  which forces  $p_1 - 1 = 2 \implies p_1 = 3$ ,  $p_2 -1 \mid n$  which forces  $p_2 - 1 \in \{p_1 , 2p_1\}$  which gives a valid  $p_2 = 7$ ,  $p_3 -1 \mid n \implies p_3 - 1 \in \{p_1, p_2, 2p_1, 2p_2, p_1p_2, 2p_1p_2\}$  giving a valid  $p_3 = 43$ ,  $p_4 -1 \mid n \implies p_4 \in \{2p_1p_3, 2p_2p_3, 2p_1p_2p_3\}$  (check) giving no valid solutions.

To clonclude, we have  $n\in \{6, 42 , 1806\}$ .

If no odd prime divides  $n$  then  $n=2$  is only possible which works.</details>

stem_md: Consider five points on a circle. For every three of them, we draw the perpendicular from the centroid of the triangle they determine to the line through the remaining two points. Prove that the ten lines thus formed are concurrent.
solution_md:
Let  $M$  be center of mass of this  $5$  points. Let  $X$  be centroid of some triangle and  $Y$  be midpoint of chord with two other points. Then if line  $OM$  intersects line drawn through  $X$  at point  $P$ , then  $\frac{OM}{MP}=\frac{MY}{MX}=\frac{3}{2}$ , so position of  $P$  is uniquely determined by the position of points  $O,M$ . (if  $M=O$ , then  $P=O$ ).
Generalization of this problem is in plane geometry by V. Prasolov (problem 14.13): on a circle,  $n$  points are given. Through the center of mass of  $n-2$  points a straight line is drawn perpendicularly to the chord that connects the two remaining points. Prove that all such straight lines intersect at one point.

stem_md: Determine all pairs  $(a,b)$  of positive integers with the following property: all of the terms of the sequence  $(a^n+b^n+1)_{n\geqslant 1}$  have a greatest common divisor  $d>1.$
solution_md:
Let  $p$  be a prime such that  $p\mid a^n+b^n+1$  for  $n\ge 1$ . Using
\[
a^3+b^3+1 - 3ab = (a+b+1)(a^2+b^2+1-ab-a-b)
\]
we get  $p\mid 3ab$ . Suppose first that  $p\mid a$  (the case  $p\mid b$  is symmetric). Then,  $p\mid a+b+1$  forces  $b\equiv -1\pmod{p}$  which together with  $p\mid a^2+b^2+1\equiv 2\pmod{p}$  forces  $p=2$ . So,  $(a,b)=(2k,2\ell-1),(2\ell-1,2k)$ , where  $k,\ell\ge 1$  are arbitrary are both solution families.

stem_md: Determine all functions  $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$  such that \[f(xy-1)+f(x)f(y)=2xy-1,\]for any real numbers  $x{}$  and  $y{}.$
solution_md:
Determine all functions $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ such that \[f(xy-1)+f(x)f(y)=2xy-1,\]for any real numbers $x{}$ and $y{}.$
Let $P(x,y)$ be the assertion $f(xy-1)+f(x)f(y)=2xy-1$ Let $c=f(1)$ If $f(0)\ne 0$ , $P(x,0)$ $\implies$ $f(x)$ constant, which is never a solution. So $f(0)=0$ $P(0,0)$ $\implies$ $f(-1)=-1$ $P(1,1)$ $\implies$ $c=\pm 1$ Subtracting $P(x,1)$ from $P(-x,-1)$ , we get $f(-x)=-cf(x)$ Subtracting $P(x,y)$ from $P(xy,1)$ , we get new assertion $Q(x,y)$ : $f(x)f(y)=cf(xy)$ If $f(u)=0$ for some $u\ne 0$ , $Q(x,u)$ implies $f(ux)=0$ $\forall x$ and so $f\equiv 0$ , which is not a solution. So $f(x)=0$ $\iff$ $x=0$ $Q(x,x)$ implies $\frac{f(x)}c$ is multiplicative and positive $\forall x>0$ and so $g(x)=\ln \frac{f(e^x)}c$ is additive If $g(x)$ is not linear, its graph is dense in $\mathbb R^2$ and so graph of $f(x)$ is : Either dense in $\mathbb R_{>0}\times \mathbb R_{>0}$ if $c=1$ Either dense in $\mathbb R_{>0}\times \mathbb R_{<0}$ if $c=-1$ But $P(x,x)$ $\implies$ $f(x^2-1)\le 2x^2-1$ and so contradiction with both cases So $g(x)$ is linear and $f(x)=cx^a$ $\forall x>0$ for some real $a$ Then $P(2,1)$ implies $c+2^a=3$ and so : If $c=1$ : $a=1$ and $f(x)=x$ $\forall x\ge 0$ and $f(-x)=-cf(x)=-f(x)$ imply $\boxed{\text{S1 : }f(x)=x\quad\forall x}$ , which indeed fits If $c=-1$ : $a=2$ and $f(x)=-x^2$ $\forall x\ge 0$ and $f(-x)=-cf(x)=f(x)$ imply $\boxed{\text{S2 : }f(x)=-x^2\quad\forall x}$ , which indeed fits

stem_md: Determine the digits  $0\leqslant c\leqslant 9$  such that for any positive integer  $k{}$  there exists a positive integer  $n$  such that the last  $k{}$  digits of  $n^9$  are equal to  $c{}.$
solution_md:
We cannot have  $c=2,4,6,8$ , because last four digits would have to be divisible by  $16$ , but in each of this cases numbers  $2222, 4444, 6666, 8888$  are not. Similarly, we can see that  $c=5$  leads to contradiction.
Now, assume that  $c$  is coprime to  $10$ . We know that  $9$  is coprime with  $\phi(5^n)$  and  $\phi(2^n)$  for all  $n$ , so function  $f(x)=x^9$  is bijective on integers relatively prime to  $10^n$  (we count modulo  $10^n$ ). To see that this function is bijective, we can also see that  $a^9\equiv b^9\mod 5^n$  iff  $5^n$  divides  $(a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2)(a^6+a^3b^3+b^6)$ , but  $5$  cannot divide neither  $a^2+ab+b^2$ , nor  $a^6+a^3b^3+b^6$  if  $ab$  is not divisible by  $5$ , so we would have to have  $a\equiv b\mod5^n$ . The same argument works modulo  $2^n$ . Therefore, we can have  $c=1,3,7,9$ . Obviously, we can also have  $c=0$ , so our answer is  $c\in\{0,1,3,7,9\}$ .

stem_md:
Six boys and six girls are participating at a tango course. They meet every evening for three weeks (a total of 21 times). Each evening, at least one boy-girl pair is selected to dance in front of the others. At the end of the three weeks, every boy-girl pair has been selected at least once. Prove that there exists a person who has been selected on at least 5 distinct evenings.

*Note:* a person can be selected twice on the same evening.
solution_md: Let  $a_i,b_i$  be number of boys and girls dancing on  $i-th$  day, respectively. Then at  $i-th$  day there can be at most  $a_ib_i$  dances. If  $a_1+a_2+...+a_{21}>24$  or  $b_1+b_2+...+b_{21}>24$ , then we are done by Dirichlet's theorem, so let us assume that this inequalities aren't true. We will prove that in such situation  $a_1b_1+a_2b_2+...+a_{21}b_{21}\leq36$  and there is only one equality case. By rearreagment inequality, we know that sum of  $a_ib_i$  is the greatest if  $a_i,b_i$  are ordered in the same way, so without loss of generality  $a_1\geq a_2\geq...\geq a_{21}$  and  $b_1\geq b_2\geq...\geq b_{21}$ . From inequalities about sums of  $a_i$  and  $b_i$  we can see that  $a_i=b_i=1$  for all  $i>3$  and  $(a_1,a_2,a_3),(b_1,b_2,b_3)\in\{(4,1,1),(3,2,1),(2,2,2)\}$ . By checking all possibilities, we can see that  $a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3\leq18$  and equality can hold only if  $(a_1,a_2,a_3)=(b_1,b_2,b_3)=(4,1,1)$ . This means that  $a_1b_1+a_2b_2+...+a_{21}b_{21}\leq18+a_4b_4+...+a_{21}b_{21}=36$ , but on the other hand, we know that each boy danced with each girl, so  $a_1b_1+...a_{21}b_{21}\geq36$ . Hence, we have to have  $a_1b_1+...+a_{21}b_{21}=36$ , but this can only happen if  $(a_1,...,a_{21})=(b_1,...,b_{21})=(4,1,1,...,1)$ . This situation gives us that except first day, on each day only one boy and one girl were dancing, so people who didn't dance on first day had to be selected at least  $6$  times, so we have our problem.

stem_md:
Let  $n$  be a positive integer. In how many ways can we mark cells on an  $n\times n$  board such that no two rows and no two columns have the same number of marked cells?

*Selim Bahadir, Turkey*
solution_md:
Basically the same as above, just adding it for storage.
-------------------------------------------------------
Let a valid arrangement a marking of cells which satisfies the problem conditions. Let the number of valid arrangements for an  $n\times n$  board be  $f(n)$  and moreover, denote the number of valid arrangements in which every column and every row contains atleast one marked cell by  $f_0(n)$ .
Assign coordinates from  $1$  to  $n$  to the rows and the columns, such that the bottom left corner has coordinates  $(1,1)$ .
Let  $r_i, c_i$  be the number of marked cells in the  $i$ -th row, respectively the  $i$ -th column.
Notice that swapping any two consecutive rows or columns in a valid arrangement gives a valid arrangement. 
If we  have a row  $i$  with no marked cells. This implies that we have a column with no marked cells, otherwise we need to have a column  $j$  in which all the cells are marked, consequently  $(i,j)$  is marked, contradiction. Thus,  $r_1, r_2, \dots r_n$  and  $c_1, c_2, \dots c_n$  are permutations of  $0,1,\dots n-1$ . Swap the rows and columns such that  $r_n=c_n=0$ . Then in the  $(n-1) \times (n-1)$  square whose bottom left corner coincides with the bottom left corner of the original board, we need to make a valid arrangement using the numbers from  $1$  to  $n-1$ , thus  $f_0(n-1)$  such valid arrangements. By fixing one of these arrangements and moving the empty row and column we get  $n^2 f_0(n-1)$  valid arrangements for an  $n\times n$  board with an empty row and an empty column.
Similarly, if  $r_1, r_2, \dots r_n$  and  $c_1, c_2, \dots c_n$  are permutations of  $1,2, \dots n$ , by swapping until  $r_n=1$  and  $c_n=n$ , we get an  $(n-1) \times (n-1)$  square whose bottom left corner coincides with the bottom left corner of the original board and in which we need to have a valid arrangement with no empty row or empty column, so  $f_0(n-1)$  arrangements. By fixing one of these arrangements and swapping back the row with  $1$  marked cell and the column in which all cells are marked, we get  $n^2f_0(n-1)$  valid arrangements where in each row and each column there is a nonzero number of marked cells.
Notice that we can find a bijection between the set of valid arrangements where a row and a column have no marked cells and the set of valid arrangements in which all the rows and the columns have atleast one marked cell, so  $f(n)=2f_0(n)=2n^2f_0(n-1)$  and we can finish with an easy recurrence.  $\blacksquare$

candidates:
First I will make some observations and then solve the problem using induction.
We assign each row and column a number equal to how many marked squares they contain. There are N rows and N columns and N+1 possible numbers (from 0 to N). Since each row has a different number, one number is not assigned to any row. 

If that number is neither 0 nor N then there is a row with 0 marked squares and one with N marked squares. We can deduce that any column has at least one marked square and one unmarked square. Therefore, there cannot be a column with 0 or N marked squares. There are N columns and only N-1 numbers and each column has a different number so there is contradiction.

This means the unassigned number for the rows is either N (so the number unassigned for columns is also N) or 0 (so the number unassigned for columns is also 0). 

Lemma 1:  Using the fact that there is either a column and a row with N marked squares or a column and a row with 0 marked squares and also inverting the state of all squares gives us a bijection between the 2, therefore we have an equal amount of each type of configuration.

The induction statement P (N) is “There are 2*(N!)^2 configurations for a board N by N.”
For n=1 (base case), the board consists of only one square and both states of it satisfy the condition, so there are 2 ways and therefore P (1) is true.

Now, while P (N-1) is true we will prove P (N) is true too.
WLOG let’s assume the unassigned numbers are 0.  There is a column and a row with N marked squares. There are N^2 ways of choosing them.
If we delete the row and the column we are left with a N-1 by N-1 board that respects the same condition with the caveat that there is no column or row with N-1 marked squares. Since we know from P (N-1) and Lemma 1 that there are ((N-1)!)^2 such configurations, therefore there are N^2 * ((N-1)!)^2 = (N!)^2 configurations for the N by N board.
Since we can invert the state of all squares in each configuration to give us a whole different one that has a column and a row with 0 marked squares, we actually have 2*(N!)^2 configurations. Therefore P (N) is true.

stem_md: Suppose a function  $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$  satisfies  $|f(x+y)|\geqslant|f(x)+f(y)|$  for all real numbers  $x$  and  $y$ . Prove that equality always holds. Is the conclusion valid if the sign of the inequality is reversed?
solution_md:
Let  $P(x,y)$  denotes the assertion that  $|f(x+y)|\ge |f(x)+f(y)|$ . Note first that  $P(0,0)$  yields  $f(0)=0$ . Further,  $P(x,-x)$  yields  $0\ge |f(x)+f(-x)|$ , thus  $f(-x)=-f(x)$  for all  $x$ . Now, we inspect  $P(x+y,-x)$  and  $P(x+y,-y)$  to get
\begin{align*}
|f(x)|\ge |f(x+y)-f(x)| \implies f(x)^2 &\ge f(x+y)^2 -2f(x+y)f(y)+f(y)^2 
|f(y)|\ge |f(x+y)-f(x)| \implies f(y)^2 &\ge f(x+y)^2 -2f(x+y)f(x)+f(x)^2.
\end{align*}
Summing these up, we find that
\[
f(x+y)\bigl(f(x)+f(y)\bigr)\ge f(x+y)^2.
\]
In particular, for every  $x,y$ ,  ${\rm sgn}(f(x+y)) = {\rm sgn}(f(x)+f(y))$ . We are now ready for conclusion. Assume first  $f(x+y)\ge 0$ . Then,  $f(x)+f(y)\ge f(x+y)\ge 0$ . So,  $|f(x)+f(y)| = f(x)+f(y) \ge f(x+y)=|f(x+y)|\ge |f(x)+f(y)|$ , yielding the desired equality. Likewise, if  $f(x+y)\le 0$ , then we find  $f(x)+f(y)\le f(x+y) \le 0$ , forcing  $|f(x)+f(y)|\ge |f(x+y)|$ , yielding the conclusion.

stem_md: Determine the greatest positive integer  $A{}$  with the following property: however we place the numbers  $1,2,\ldots, 100$  on a  $10\times 10$  board, each number appearing exactly once, we can find two numbers on the same row or column which differ by at least  $A{}$ .
solution_md:
Here is a proof that there is always a difference at least  $54$ .

The basic idea is to take two sets of "small" and "large" number, and prove with PHP that there is a line covered by both a large and a small number, so that there will be a big difference on this line.

Take the sets  $\{1, 2,..., 26\}$  and  $\{80, 81,..., 100\}$ . If the first one is covered by  $m$  rows and  $n$  columns, then  $26 \leq mn \leq  \frac{(m+n)^2} {4}$ , so  $m+n>10$  and similarly the other set is covered by more than  $9$  lines, so there is a line covered by both sets, which guarantees a difference at least  $80-26=54$ .

stem_md: Let  $x>1$  be a real number which is not an integer. For each  $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , let  $a_n=\lfloor x^{n+1}\rfloor - x\lfloor x^n\rfloor$ . Prove that the sequence  $(a_n)$  is not periodic.
solution_md:
Suppose it is indeed periodic. stem_md: Two circles intersect at points  $A\neq B$ . A line passing through  $A{}$  intersects the circles again at  $C$  and  $D$ . Let  $E$  and  $F$  be the midpoints of the arcs  $\overarc{BC}$  and  $\overarc{BD}$  which do not contain  $A{}$  and let  $M$  be the midpoint of the segment  $CD$ . Prove that  $ME$  and  $MF$  are perpendicular.
solution_md:
Pretty much the same solution as above. This was a pretty cool problem. We first need to show the following key claim. **Claim :**Points $A,F,E$ and $M$ are concyclic. *Proof :* Denote by $M'$ the second intersection of $(AEF)$ and $\overline{CAD}$ . We wish to show $(CD;M'P_{\infty})=-1$ . Now, consider an inversion centered at $A$ . Then, it suffices to show the following.
Consider $\triangle BCD$ with point $A$ on side $CD$ . Let $E$ and $F$ be the intersection of the internal $\angle BAC$ and $\angle BAD$ bisectors with sides $BC$ and $BD$ respectively. Let $M = \overline{EF} \cap \overline{CD}$ . Show that $(CD;AM)=-1$ .
We solve this as follows. Note that by the Angle Bisector Theorem we have, \[\frac{BF}{FD} \cdot \frac{DA}{AC} \cdot \frac{CE}{EB} = \frac{AB}{AD} \cdot \frac{DA}{AC} \cdot \frac{CA}{AB}=1\] which by the converse of Ceva's Theorem implies that cevians $\overline{CF}$ , $\overline{DE}$ and $\overline{AB}$ concur. Thus, by the Ceva/Menalaus picture we have $(CD;AM)=-1$ as we set out to show. Now, due to the well known fact that inversion preserves the cross ratio, we must have that $(CD;AM')=-1$ as well, and thus $M'\equiv M$ . This means $M$ indeed lies on $(AEF)$ and the claim is proved. To finish off note that since in $\angle BAC$ , $\overline{AE}$ and $\overline{AF}$ are respectively the internal and external angle bisectors, it follows that $\angle EAF = \frac{\pi}{2}$ . Thus, $\angle EMF = \frac{pi}{2}$ as well, implying that $EM \perp FM$ as desired.

stem_md: Determine all non-negative integers  $n$  for which there exist two relatively prime non-negative integers  $x$  and  $y$  and a positive integer  $k\geqslant 2$  such that  $3^n=x^k+y^k$ .
solution_md:
When  $n \leq 2$  we see that  $\exists x,y,k$  satisfied. Consider  $n \geq 3$ .
Easy to see  $k$  is odd, because when  $k$  is even we infer  $3 \mid x,y$ .
We have  $x+y \mid x^k+y^k=3^n$ , therefore  $x+y=3^q$ Using LTE theorem we have  $n=v_3(x^k+y^k)=v_3(x+y)+v_3(k)=q+v_3(k)$  $\Rightarrow v_3(k)=n-q \Rightarrow k \geq 3^{n-q}$ Since  $x+y$  is odd, WLOG  $x>y$ We have  $x^{k-1}-x^{k-2}y+x^{k-3}y^2-x^{k-4}y^3+...-xy^{k-2}+y^{k-1}>y^{k-1}$ If  $y=1$  then  $x^k=3^n-1$ . Easy to see there is no solution for this.
Therefore  $y \geq 2$ . Then  $3^n=x^k+y^k=(x+y)(x^{k-1}-x^{k-2}y+x^{k-3}y^2-x^{k-4}y^3+...-xy^{k-2}+y^{k-1})>2^{k-1}\cdot 3^q$  $\Rightarrow 2^{k-1}>3^{n-q}$ But we have  $2^{k-1} \geq k \geq 3^{n-q}$ , therefore we have contradiction.
So, only  $n=0,n=1,n=2$  are satisfied.

Let  $(a_n)_{n\geq 1}$  be a sequence for real numbers given by  $a_1=1/2$  and for each positive integer  $n$ 
\[ a_{n+1}=\frac{a_n^2}{a_n^2-a_n+1}.  \]
Prove that for every positive integer  $n$  we have  $a_1+a_2+\cdots + a_n<1$ .
solution_md: Define  $b_n = \frac{1}{a_n}$ . Then  $b_{n + 1} = b_n^2 - b_n + 1$  or \[\frac{b_{n + 1} - 1}{b_n - 1} = b_n.\] Multiplying these relations (the whole thing telescopes) we get \[b_{n + 1} = b_n\cdots b_2b_1 + 1 \Leftrightarrow \frac{1}{b_n} = \frac{1}{b_1b_2\cdots b_{n - 1}} - \frac{1}{b_1b_2\cdots b_{n}}.\] Telescoping again we get \[\frac{1}{b_1} + \frac{1}{b_2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{b_n} = 1 - \frac{1}{b_1b_2\cdots b_n}\] and we are done.

solution_md:
Note that there are exactly  $\binom{22}{2}$  pairs of birds on the same tree at a given time in total.

But  $230 < 231 = \binom{22}{2}$ , contradiction.  $\square$

stem_md:
$BE$  and  $CF$  are the altitudes of the acute scalene  $\triangle ABC$ ,  $O$  is its circumcenter and  $M$  is the midpoint of the side  $BC$ . If point, which is symmetric to  $M$  with respect to  $O$ , lies on the line  $EF$ , find all possible values of the ratio  $\dfrac{AM}{AO}$ .
*Proposed by Fedir Yudin*
solution_md:
Let  $AO$  and  $EF$  meet at point  $K$ ,  $N$  be the midpoint of  $EF$ ,  $T$  be the projection of  $A$  on  $OM$ ,  $X,Y$  be the midpoints of  $AB,AC$  respectively,  $O'$  be the symmetric point of  $O$  with respect to  $EF$ , and lastly  $P$  be the point of intersection between the tangents of circle  $(ABC)$  at points  $B,C$ . 

We will prove that  $AM=AO\sqrt{2}$ . We have the following two Claims, which essentially solve the problem:**Claim 1:**  $AM=AO\sqrt{2}$  is equivalent to  $\sin^2 \angle A+\cos 2\angle B+\cos 2\angle C=0$ *Proof:* Note that  $AM=AO\sqrt{2}$  is equivalent to  $AM^2=2AO^2$ , and since  $TM^2-TO^2=AM^2-AO^2$ , this is equivalent to $TM^2-TO^2=AO^2$ .

Note that $OM \cdot OP=OB^2=OA^2=TM^2-TO^2=MO(TM+TO),$ and so the above relation is equivalent to  $OP=TM+TO,$  that is  $PM=2TO$ . However, $PM=MB\tan \angle A=\dfrac{a\tan \angle A}{2}$ and $2TO=2AO\sin \angle TAO=2AO\cos(\angle B-\angle C)=\dfrac{a\cos(\angle B-\angle C)}{\sin \angle A}$ Therefore,  $PM=2TO$  is equivalent to  $\dfrac{a\tan \angle A}{2}=\dfrac{a\cos(\angle B-\angle C)}{\sin \angle A},$ that is  $\sin^2 \angle A=2\cos \angle A\cos(\angle B-\angle C),$  and since  $2\cos x\cos y=\cos(x+y)+\cos(x-y),$  the previous equality is equivalent to $\sin^2\angle A=-\cos 2\angle C-\cos 2 \angle B,$ as desired  $\blacksquare$ **Claim 2:**  $O' \in EF \Longleftrightarrow \sin^2 \angle A+\cos 2\angle B+\cos 2\angle C=0$ *Proof:* Note that  $O' \in EF$  is equivalent to  $ON=OM$ . Applying the median formula in triangle  $OEF,$  we have that $4ON^2=2OF^2+2OE^2-EF^2=2(OX^2+OY^2+XF^2+EY^2)-EF^2=2(2R^2-AX^2-AY^2+XF^2+EY^2)-EF^2,$ and so the above relation is equivalent to  $2(2R^2-AX^2-AY^2+XF^2+EY^2)-EF^2=4OM^2,$ that is $2AX^2+2AY^2-2XF^2-2EY^2+EF^2=a^2$ Note that  $EF/BC=AF/AC=\cos \angle A$ , and so  $EF^2=a^2\cos^2 \angle A$ , hence the previous relation is equivalent to $2AX^2+2AY^2-2XF^2-2EY^2=a^2\sin^2 \angle A$ .

Now, note that $2AX^2+2AY^2-2XF^2-2EY^2=2(BX^2-XF^2)+2(CY^2-EY^2)=2BF(2BX-BF)+2CE(2YC-EC),$ and so we finally have $2BF(2BX-BF)+2CE(2YC-EC)=a^2\sin^2\angle A$ Dividing by  $2a^2$ , we easily obtain that the above equality rewrites as $\dfrac{\sin^2\angle A}{2}=(\dfrac{c}{a}-\cos \angle B)\cos \angle B+(\dfrac{b}{a}-\cos \angle C)\cos \angle C,$ and since  $b\cos \angle C+c\cos \angle B=BV+CV=a,$  with  $V$  being the foot of the  $A-$ altitude, we have that the previous equality is equivalent to $2-2\cos^2 \angle B-2\cos^2 \angle C=\sin^2\angle A,$ which, in light of the identity  $\cos 2x=2\cos^2x-1$  gives the desired result  $\blacksquare$ Now, combining both claims, we may easily finish.

stem_md: Let  $n \geq 3$  be positive integer such that  $a \in \mathbb{R}-\{0\}$ . Prove that if  $ z\in \mathbb{C}-\mathbb{R}$  be the root of  $x^n+ax+1=0$  then  $|z| \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt[n]{n-1}}$
solution_md:
Let $n \geq 3$ be positive integer such that $a \in \mathbb{R}-\{0\}$ . Prove that if $ z\in \mathbb{C}-\mathbb{R}$ be the root of $x^n+ax+1=0$ then $|z| \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt[n]{n-1}}$
Let $z=re^{it}$ with $r\ge 0$ and $\sin t\ne 0$ such a root. $z$ solution of $x^n+ax+1=0$ is equivalent to $r^n\sin nt+ar\sin t=0$ and $r^n\cos nt+ar\cos t +1 =0$ The first equation gives $a=-\frac{r^n\sin nt}{r\sin t}$ (btw, this means $\sin nt\ne 0$ too) Plugging this in second equation, we get $r^n\sin (n-1)t=\sin t$ (and so $\sin (n-1)t\ne 0$ ) And so $\sin t,\sin (n-1)t,\sin nt\ne 0$ and $r^n=\frac{\sin t}{\sin (n-1)t}$ And it remains to prove that $\frac{\sin t}{\sin (n-1)t}>0$ $\implies$ $\frac{\sin t}{\sin (n-1)t}\ge \frac 1{n-1}$ Which is not very difficult for example with induction.

If  $f(x)=f(y)$ , we get  $xa=ya \implies xab=yab$ , or  $x=y$ . Thus,  $f$  is injective, and, since  $M$  is finite, surjective. Thus, there is  $c \in M$  with  $ca=e$ . Computing  $cab$  in 2 different ways gives  $b=c$ , so  $ba=e$ , contradiction.

Left multiply by  $a^{min\{n,q\}}$  and right multiply by  $b^{min\{m,p\}}$  the given relation. The idea is that all of the  $a$ 's on one side of the equation will cancel out, and the same for the  $b$ 's. Assume FTSOC that their powers are nonzero. We distinguish 2 cases:**<u>Case 1</u>**: The  $a$ 's and the  $b$ 's are on the same side of the equation
In other words,  $b^{|n-q|}a^{|m-p|}=e$ . 
Denote by  $u=|n-q|, v=|m-p|$  and assume WLOG  $u \leq v$  (The other case is similar)
If  $u \neq v$ , left multiply by  $a^u$ , and right multiply by  $b^{v-1}$  to get  $a=b^{v-u-1}$ , so  $ab=ba$ , contradiction!
Therefore,  $u=v$ . Left multiply by  $a^{u-1}$  and right multiply by  $b^{u-1}$  to get  $ba=e$ , contradiction!
Thus, we must have one of  $u,v$  to be  $0$ , but if, say  $u=0$  and  $v \neq 0$ , then  $a^v=e$ , so  $b=a^{v-1}$ , and  $ba=e$ , contradiction!
Thus,  $u=v=0$ , and we are done in this case**<u>Case 2:</u>**  $a$  and  $b$  appear on distinct sides of the equation
In other words,  $a^v=b^u$ . Left multiply by  $a^{u-1}$  to get  $b=a^{u+v-1}$ , so  $a,b$  commute, contradiction! Thus,  $u=0$ , and likewise  $v=0$ , completing the proof.

solution_md:
Classical, we have  $\int_0^\pi (f+a\cos x+b\sin x)^2 dx\ge 0$  for all  $a,b\in R$ .
Hence  $\int_0^\pi f^2 dx+{\pi\over 2}(a^2+b^2)+2(a+b)\ge 0$  and  $\int_0^\pi f^2 dx+{\pi\over 2}((a+2/\pi)^2+(b+2/\pi)^2-8/\pi^2)\ge 0$ .
Hence  $\int_0^\pi f^2 dx\ge 4/\pi$  and equality for  $f=2/\pi(\sin x+\cos x)$ .

stem_md: Let  $K$  be a finite field. Find the set of integers  $n \ge 2$  having the property that any  $n$ -th degree polynomial in  $K[X]$  with no roots in  $K$  is irreducible over  $K.$
solution_md:
For  $n=2,3$  it is clear since only the partitions  $2=1+1,3=1+2$  are possible for the degrees.
Write  $|K|=p^k$  where  $p$  is prime and  $k\ge 1$ . Then  $K$  embeds into  $L:=F_{p^{2k}}$ . Choose  $a\in L\setminus K$  then  $[K(a):K]=2$  and  $g:=f_K^a\in K[x]$  is irreducible of degree 2. In the same way we can find  $h\in K[x]$  irr of degree 3.
Every integer  $n\ge 4$  can be written in the form  $n=2k+3l$  where  $k,l\ge 0$  and we note that  $k+l>1$ .
Then  $\phi=g^k h^l$  has degree  $n$ , no roots in  $K$  and it is reducible. Hence  $n\ge 4$  does not have the required property.

stem_md: Let  $f: \mathbb{Z}_+ \to \mathbb{Z}_+$  be defined by   $$ f(n)=\mathrm{the~number~of~perfect~squares~in~the~interval~}[n^2,2n^2]. $$  Prove that  $f$  is increasing and surjective.
solution_md:
Btw did you mean nondecreasing rather than increasing?

Let  $k^{2} \in [n^{2}, 2n^{2}].$  Then, we get that  $n \le k \le nsqrt{2},$  so  $f(n) = \lfloor n\sqrt{2}\rfloor-n+1 = 1+\lfloor n(\sqrt{2}-1)\rfloor.$  Since  $g \equiv \lfloor x\rfloor $   is a nondecreasing function, we find that our function  $f$  is nonincreasing. 

Next, we claim that  $\lfloor (n+1)(\sqrt{2}-1)\rfloor \le \lfloor n(\sqrt{2}-1)\rfloor+1,$  which clearly shows the result (as no positive integers ca be skipped). Assume for the sake of contradiction that  $\lfloor (n+1)(\sqrt{2}-1)\rfloor \ge \lfloor n(\sqrt{2}-1)\rfloor+2.$  Let  $n(\sqrt{2}-1)=m,$  then  $\lfloor m+\sqrt{2}-1\rfloor \ge \lfloor m\rfloor +2$ . Notice that  $\lfloor m+1 \rfloor = \lfloor m\rfloor +1,$  so then we would have  $\lfloor m+\sqrt{2}-1\rfloor \ge \lfloor m+1 \rfloor,$  a clear contradiction to the fact that  $\lfloor x\rfloor$  is nondecreasing. Thus, in fact our claim is true.

solution_md:
Let $A \in \mathcal{M}_{3,2}(\mathbb{C})$ and $B \in \mathcal{M}_{2,3}(\mathbb{C})$ be such that $AB= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 0 & 0 & 2 0 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.$ Calculate $\det(BA).$

stem_md: Let  $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$  be a surjective function with the property that for any divergent sequence of real numbers  $(x_n)_{n \ge 1},$  the sequence  $(f(x_n))_{n \ge 1}$  is also divergent. Prove that  $f$  is continuous.
solution_md: Suppose  $f(a)=f(b)$  and set  $x_n=a,b,a,b,\cdots$  Then  $f(x_n)$  converges,  $x_n$  converges and  $a=b$ . Hence  $f$  is a bijection. Now suppose  $f(x_n)\rightarrow b$  and set  $a:=f^{-1}(b)$ . Then we consider  $y_n=x_1,a,x_2,a,\cdots$  and  $f(y_n)\rightarrow b$ . Hence  $x_n\rightarrow a$  and we have shown that  $g:=f^{-1}$  is a continuous bijection from  $R$  to  $R$ . Then  $g$  is strictly monotone and a homeomorphism. Hence  $f=g^{-1}$  is continuous.

candidates:
Step 1: Prove \(f\) is injective.
Assume, for contradiction, that \(f\) is not injective. Then there exist distinct \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(f(a) = f(b) = L\) for some \(L \in \mathbb{R}\). Define the sequence:
\[
x_n = \begin{cases} 
a & \text{if } n \text{ is odd}, 
b & \text{if } n \text{ is even}.
\end{cases}
\]
Since \(a \neq b\), the sequence \((x_n)\) is divergent (it oscillates between \(a\) and \(b\)). However, \(f(x_n) = L\) for all \(n\), so \((f(x_n))\) converges to \(L\), contradicting the hypothesis. Thus, \(f\) is injective.**Step 2:** Prove \(f\) is bijective.
By hypothesis, \(f\) is surjective. Since \(f\) is also injective (Step 1), it is bijective. Therefore, \(f\) has a well-defined inverse function \(g = f^{-1}: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\).**Step 3:** Prove \(g\) is continuous.
Let \((y_n)\) be a sequence in \(\mathbb{R}\) converging to some \(y \in \mathbb{R}\). Define \(x_n = g(y_n)\). We need to show that \(x_n \to g(y)\).

-**Boundedness of \((x_n)\):**
  If \((x_n)\) is unbounded, it contains a subsequence \((x_{n_k})\) such that \(|x_{n_k}| \to \infty\) (divergent). By the hypothesis, \((f(x_{n_k})) = (y_{n_k})\) is divergent. However, \((y_n)\) converges to \(y\), so its subsequence \((y_{n_k})\) converges to \(y\), a contradiction. Thus, \((x_n)\) is bounded.

- **Convergence of \((x_n)\) to \(g(y)\):** 
  Assume, for contradiction, that \(x_n \not\to g(y)\). Then there exist \(\epsilon > 0\) and a subsequence \((x_{n_k})\) such that \(|x_{n_k} - g(y)| \geq \epsilon\) for all \(k\). Since \((x_n)\) is bounded, \((x_{n_k})\) is bounded and has a convergent subsequence \((x_{n_{k_j}})\) by the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem. Let \(x_{n_{k_j}} \to L\) as \(j \to \infty\). Then \(|L - g(y)| \geq \epsilon\), so \(L \neq g(y)\).  

  Define a new sequence:
  \[
  z_j = \begin{cases} 
  x_{n_{k_j}} & \text{if } j \text{ is odd}, 
  g(y) & \text{if } j \text{ is even}.
  \end{cases}
  \]
  - The sequence \((z_j)\) is divergent because the odd terms converge to \(L\) and the even terms converge to \(g(y) \neq L\).  
  - Now, \(f(z_j) = \begin{cases} 
    f(x_{n_{k_j}}) = y_{n_{k_j}} & \text{if } j \text{ is odd}, 
    f(g(y)) = y & \text{if } j \text{ is even}.
    \end{cases}\)  
    As \(j \to \infty\), \(y_{n_{k_j}} \to y\) (since \(y_n \to y\)), and for even \(j\), \(f(z_j) = y\). Thus, \(f(z_j) \to y\), so \((f(z_j))\) converges.  

  This contradicts the hypothesis, as \((z_j)\) is divergent but \((f(z_j))\) converges. Therefore, \(x_n \to g(y)\), and \(g\) is continuous.

 **Step 4:** Prove \(f\) is continuous.
Since \(g = f^{-1}\) is a continuous bijection from \(\mathbb{R}\) to \(\mathbb{R}\), it is strictly monotonic (a standard result for continuous bijections on \(\mathbb{R}\)). The inverse of a strictly monotonic continuous function is continuous. Thus, \(f = g^{-1}\) is continuous.

stem_md: Let  $A, B \in M_2(\mathbb{R})$  such as  $det(AB+BA)\leq 0$ . Prove that   $$ det(A^2+B^2)\geq 0 $$
solution_md:
Solved it using the property:
If  $X, Y \in M_2(\mathbb{R})$ , then  $det(X+Y)+det(X-Y)=2 \cdot (detX+detY)$ .
Applying it to  $X=A^2+B^2$  and  $Y=AB+BA$ , we get   $$ det(A+B)^2+det(A-B)^2=2 \cdot (det(A^2+B^2)+det(AB+BA)) \Leftrightarrow $$     $$ det(A^2+B^2)=\frac{det^2(A+B)+det^2(A-B)-2det(AB+BA)}{2} \geq 0 $$

stem_md:
$ a,b,c,d \in [0,1]$  and  $ x,y,z,t \in [0, \frac{1}{2}]$  and  $ a+b+c+d=x+y+z+t=1$ .prove that:
 $ (i)$   $ ax+by+cz+dt$   $ \geq$   $ min( {\frac{a+b}{2} , \frac{b+c}{2} , \frac{c+d}{2} , \frac{d+a}{2} , \frac{a+c}{2} , \frac{b+d}{2} )}$ 
 $ (ii)$   $ ax+by+cz+dt$   $ \geq$   $ 54abcd$
solution_md:
i) WLOG  $ a \ge b \ge c \ge d$ . Then  $ \frac {1}{2}(c \plus{} d) \le td \plus{} cz \plus{} (1 \minus{} t \minus{} d)b \le td \plus{} cz \plus{} by \plus{} ax$ 

ii) It suffices to show that  $ \frac {c \plus{} d}{2} \ge 54abcd$ .

It then suffices to show that  $ c \plus{} d \ge 108(\frac {a \plus{} b}{2})^2(\frac {c \plus{} d}{2})^2$ 
 $ \leftrightarrow 4(c \plus{} d) \ge 27(1 \minus{} (c \plus{} d))^2(c \plus{} d)^2$ 
 $ \leftrightarrow 4 \ge 27(1 \minus{} (c \plus{} d))^2(c \plus{} d)^2$ 

Which is true since  $ 27((1 \minus{} (c \plus{} d))(c \plus{} d))^2 \le 27(\frac {c \plus{} d \plus{} (1 \minus{} (c \plus{} d))}{2})^4 \equal{} \frac {27}{16} < 4$ 

The stronger inequality  $ ax \plus{} by \plus{} cz \plus{} dt \ge 54(\sqrt {ab})cd$ , was probably intended, since then equality can actually be obtained (use the same method as above).

I assume the first 1990 has to be 1989. Write  $x-1991=y$  then  $\sqrt{{y+1984}\over {1989}}+\sqrt{{y+1985}\over {1990}}+\sqrt{{y+1986}\over {1991}}=\sqrt{{y+2}\over 7}+\sqrt{{y+1}\over 6}+\sqrt{y\over 5}$ We have  $y\ge 0$  for any solution.

stem_md: Let  $I \subset \mathbb{R}$  be a nondegenerate interval and  $f:I \to \mathbb{R}$  a differentiable function. We denote  $J= \left\{ \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} : a,b \in I, a<b \right\}.$  Prove that: $a)$   $J$  is an interval; $b)$   $J \subset f'(I),$  and the set  $f'(I) \setminus J$  contains at most two elements; $c)$  Using parts  $a)$  and  $b),$  deduce that  $f'$  has the intermediate value property.
solution_md:
$a)$  It is enough to prove that for any  $u,v \in J$  we have  $[u,v] \subseteq J$  (i.e. that  $J$  is convex). <details><summary>Details</summary>Once this is proved, let  $(x_n), (y_n) \subset I$  be strictly monotone sequences that converge respectively to  $\inf J$  and  $\sup J.$  Then  $(\inf J, \sup J) = \bigcup_k [x_k,y_k] \subseteq J \subseteq [\inf J, \sup J],$  showing that  $J$  is an interval with endpoints  $\inf J$  and  $\sup J.$</details>

Let  $u,v \in J.$  Then there exist  $a,b,c,d$  such that  $u=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$  and  $v= \frac{f(d)-f(c)}{d-c}.$  We can assume WLOG  $a<b$  (otherwise swap them) and likewise  $d<c.$  Consider the function  $g:[0,1] \to \mathbb{R},$    $$ g(t)=\frac{f((1-t)b+td)-f((1-t)a+tc)}{(1-t)(b-a)+t(d-c)}. $$   This function is continuous and we have  $g(0)=u$  and  $g(1)=v,$  so  $[u,v] \subseteq g([0,1]) \subseteq J,$  by IVT. $b)$  For any  $a<b$  in  $I$  there is  $c \in I$  such that  $f'(c)= \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a},$  by MVT. This shows that  $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} \in f'(I)$  for any  $a,b \in I,$  so  $J \subseteq f'(I).$ Let  $p= \inf J$  and  $q= \sup J.$  For any  $s \in I$  we have  $f'(s)= \lim_{x \to s} \frac{f(x)-f(s)}{x-s},$  but  $p \le \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} \le q,$  for any  $a,b \in I,$  so  $p \le f'(s) \le q.$  This shows that  $f'(I) \subseteq [p,q].$  Combining this with  $(p,q) \subseteq J$  (established in "Details" above), we get  $f'(I) \setminus J \subseteq \{p,q\}.$  $c)$  Part  $b)$  shows that  $f'(I)$  is an interval (to be more precise,  $f'(I)$  is an interval with endpoints  $p$  and  $q$ ). The restriction of  $f$  to any subinterval is still differentiable, so, applying the result from  $b)$  to these restrictions of  $f,$  we get that  $f'$  transforms intervals into intervals. This trivially implies IVP (in fact it is equivalent to it).

stem_md:
a) Let  $f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_n: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$  be periodic functions such that the function  $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R},$   $f=f_1+f_2+\ldots+f_n$  has finite limit at  $\infty.$  Prove that  $f$  is constant.

b) If  $a_1,a_2,a_3$  are real numbers such that  $a_1 \cos(a_1x) + a_2 \cos (a_2x) + a_3 \cos(a_3x) \ge 0$  for every  $x \in \mathbb{R},$  then  $a_1a_2a_3=0.$
solution_md:
a) With induction. Suppose  $f$  is periodic with period  $p>0$  and  $f(\infty)=c$ . Then  $f(x)=f(x+kp)\rightarrow c$  as  $k\rightarrow \infty$ . Hence  $f\equiv c$ . Now suppose  $n>1$ , that it's true for  $1,n-1$  and let  $p>0$  be a period for  $f_n$ .
Then  $g(x):=f(x+p)-f(x)=\sum_1^{n-1} (f_k(x+p)-f_k(x))$  has limit 0 as  $x\rightarrow \infty$  and each  $f_k(x+p)-f_k(x)$  is periodic. Hence  $g$  is constant,  $g\equiv 0$  and  $f$  has period  $p$ . By the  $n=1$  case, we find that  $f$  is constant.
b) Set  $f=\sum_1^3 \sin a_kx$  then  $f'\ge 0$  everywhere and  $f$  is bounded. Hence  $f$  has a finite limit at  $\infty$  and  $f$  is constant. Since  $f$  is odd, we have  $\sum_1^3 \sin a_k x\equiv 0$ . 
Hence we consider the case  $\sin ax+\sin bx=\sin cx$  for all  $x$  with  $abc\not=0$ .
Taking derivatives in  $x=0$  we find  $a+b=c$ . Also  $2\sin (cx/2)\cos ((a-b)x/2)=2\sin (cx/2)\cos (cx/2)$  for all  $x$ . Hence  $\cos ((a-b)x/2)=\cos(cx/2)$  for all  $x$  by continuity. Taking double derivatives in  $x=0$  we find  $|a-b|=|c|$ . If  $a-b=c$  then  $a=b+c=c-b\implies b=0$ . If  $b-a=c$  then  $b=a+c=c-a\implies a=0$ . Contradiction.

stem_md: Prove that a group  $G$  in which exactly two elements other than the identity commute with each other is isomorphic to  $\mathbb{Z}/3 \mathbb{Z}$  or  $S_3.$
solution_md:
We are given that in the group  $G$ , there are exactly two non-identity elements that commute with each other. That is, there exist distinct elements  $a, b \in G$ ,  $a \neq e$ ,  $b \neq e$ , such that  $ab = ba$ , and all other pairs of non-identity elements in  $G$  do not commute. Our goal is to determine all such groups  $G$  up to isomorphism.

Step 1: The group cannot be abelian

Suppose  $G$  were abelian. Then every pair of elements in  $G$  commutes. In particular, all non-identity elements would commute with each other, violating the condition that only two non-identity elements commute. Therefore,  $G$  must be a non-abelian group.

Step 2: Consider the number of commuting elements

We are told that exactly two non-identity elements commute. Denote these two elements by  $x$  and  $y$ . Then  $xy = yx$ . We may assume  $x \neq y$  and  $x, y \neq e$ .

Observation: Any subgroup generated by  $x$  and  $y$  must be abelian, since  $x$  and  $y$  commute. But since no other pair of non-identity elements in  $G$  commutes, this subgroup cannot contain more than three elements (identity and  $x$ ,  $y$ ). Otherwise, we would get additional pairs of commuting non-identity elements.

Thus, the subgroup  $\langle x, y \rangle$  must be of order 3. The only group of order 3 is the cyclic group  $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ .

Step 3: Consider possible orders of  $G$ Let us now determine the possible orders of  $G$ . Since  $G$  is finite (implied by the condition), suppose  $|G| = n$ . Let us consider the possible prime divisors of  $n$ .

By Cauchy's Theorem, for any prime  $p$  dividing  $|G|$ , there exists an element of order  $p$ , and hence a cyclic subgroup of order  $p$ .

Important point: Any cyclic subgroup of order  $p > 3$  contains more than two non-identity elements (specifically,  $p - 1$  of them), and these all commute with each other. That would contradict the assumption that only two non-identity elements in  $G$  commute.

Hence, the only primes that can divide  $|G|$  are  $2$  and  $3$ . That is,
\[
|G| = 2^m \cdot 3^n \quad \text{for some integers } m, n \geq 0.
\]

Now suppose  $m \geq 2$ . Then  $G$  would have a subgroup of order  $4$  by Cauchy's Theorem and the Sylow theorems. All groups of order  $4$  are abelian, so that subgroup would contain more than two non-identity elements that commute with each other, again violating the hypothesis.

Similarly, if  $n \geq 2$ , then  $G$  would have a subgroup of order  $9$ , which is abelian (since all groups of order  $9$  are abelian). Again, we would get too many commuting non-identity elements.

Therefore, we must have  $m \leq 1$  and  $n \leq 1$ . So the possible orders of  $G$  are:
\[
1, 2, 3, 6.
\]

We can eliminate some of these immediately:

  $|G| = 1$ : trivial group, no non-identity elements --- ruled out. $|G| = 2$ : cyclic of order 2 --- abelian, so all elements commute --- ruled out.

  $|G| = 3$ : cyclic of order 3. This group has two non-identity elements, and they commute (since it is abelian). This exactly matches the condition! So  $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$  is a valid example.

  $|G| = 6$ : There are exactly two groups of order 6 up to isomorphism: the cyclic group  $\mathbb{Z}_6$ , which is abelian (ruled out), and the symmetric group  $S_3$ , which is non-abelian. We now check whether  $S_3$  satisfies the condition.

Step 4: Check  $S_3$ The group  $S_3$  has six elements:
\[
S_3 = \{e, (12), (13), (23), (123), (132)\}.
\]

Among the non-identity elements, only the two 3-cycles  $(123)$  and  $(132)$  commute with each other:
\[
(123)(132) = (132)(123) = e.
\]
All transpositions (like  $(12)$  and  $(13)$ ) do not commute with each other, and neither do they commute with the 3-cycles. Thus, in  $S_3$ , the only pair of non-identity elements that commute is  $\{(123), (132)\}$ .

Therefore,  $S_3$  satisfies the condition.

Conclusion

The only groups in which exactly two non-identity elements commute with each other are:
\[
\mathbb{Z}_3 \quad \text{and} \quad S_3.
\]

Important note: **These are not the only groups satisfying the given condition but the only one up to isomorhism.**

stem_md: Let  $A$  be a commutative ring with  $0 \neq 1$  such that for any  $x \in A \setminus \{0\}$  there exist positive integers  $m,n$  such that  $(x^m+1)^n=x.$  Prove that any endomorphism of  $A$  is an automorphism.
solution_md:
Let  $f$  be an endomorphism of  $A.$  It follows from the condition given in your problem that  $A$  is a field and so  $\ker f=(0),$  i.e.  $f$  is injective. Choosing  $x=1$  in the condition, shows that the characteristic of  $A$  is  $p > 0.$  Let  $0 \ne a \in A.$  So  $a=(a^m+1)^n$  for some positive integers  $m,n.$  Consider the polynomial  $g(x):=(x^m+1)^n-x \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]$  and let  $S$  be the set of roots of  $g$  in  $A.$  Then  $S$  is finite,  $a \in S,$  and  $f(s) \in S$  for all  $s \in S.$  Thus, since  $f$  is injective,  $S=f(S)$  and so  $a=f(s)$  for some  $s \in S,$  proving that  $f$  is surjective hence an automorphism.

A trivial generalization of your problem is that every endomorphism of an algebraic field extension is an automorphism.

stem_md: Prove that  $ \forall x\in \mathbb{R} $  ,  $ \cos ^7x+\cos ^7(x+\frac {2\pi}{3})+\cos ^7(x+\frac {4\pi}{3})=\frac {63}{64}\cos 3x $
solution_md:
We know that  $cos^n(x)$  is a linear combination of  $1,cos(x),cos(2x),\dots,cos(nx)$ .
The expression on the left is invariant under  $x \to x+ 2\pi/3$  so that only  $1, cos(3x), cos(6x)$  appear.
The expression changes sign under  $x \to x+\pi$  so that only  $cos(3x)$  has a nonzero coefficient.  
So the problem reduces to evaluation of the sum at some particular  $x$ , such as  $x=0$ , where the cosines are  $1, -1/2, -1/2$  and the computation is trivial.

stem_md: Let  $a,b,c\in Z$  and  $a$  be the even number and  $b$  be the odd number. Show that for every integer  $n$  there exist one positive integer   $x$  such that  $2^n\mid ax^2+bx+c$
solution_md:
Let $a,b,c\in Z$ and $a$ be the even number and $b$ be the odd number. Show that for every integer $n$ there exist one positive integer $x$ such that $2^n\mid ax^2+bx+c$
Consider the values of the polynomial $f\left(x\right)=ax^2+bx+c$ for $x\in\left\{0;\;1;\;...;\;2^n-1\right\}$ . These are $2^n$ values, and all of them have different remainders $\mod 2^n$ ; in fact, if, for two different numbers x and y from the set $\left\{0;\;1;\;...;\;2^n-1\right\}$ , the values f(x) and f(y) would have the same remainder $\mod 2^n$ , then f(x) - f(y) would be divisible by $2^n$ , but since $f\left(x\right)-f\left(y\right)=\left(ax^2+bx+c\right)-\left(ay^2+by+c\right)=\left(x-y\right)\left(a\left(x+y\right)+b\right)$ , and since the right factor a (x + y) + b is odd (since a is even and b is odd), this would mean that the number x - y would be divisible by $2^n$ , what is impossible (since x and y are different integers between 0 and $2^n-1$ ). So the values of the polynomial $f\left(x\right)=ax^2+bx+c$ have $2^n$ different remainders $\mod 2^n$ . But there are only $2^n$ possible remainders $\mod 2^n$ , and thus all of these remainders are represented. Particularly, there must be some x such that f(x) has the remainder 0 $\mod 2^n$ . But this means that $2^n\mid f\left(x\right)$ ; in other words, $2^n\mid ax^2+bx+c$ . The problem is solved. darij
